questions.explanation: Per the lecture answer key, the correct choice is: Pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblet cells.
questions.keyConcept: Pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblet cells
options: Pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium with goblet cells

questions.text: A cataract is described as an accumulation of brownish pigment in lens fibers, leading to loss of transparency. In addition to old age, which of the following is mentioned as a cause of cataract?
questions.explanation: Per the lecture answer key, the correct choice is: Increased glucose level as in diabetes mellitus.
questions.keyConcept: Increased glucose level as in diabetes mellitus
options: Increased glucose level as in diabetes mellitus

questions.text: The inner plexiform layer of the retina contains:
questions.explanation: The inner plexiform layer is where the axons of bipolar cells synapse with the dendrites of ganglion and amacrine cells.
questions.keyConcept: The inner plexiform layer contains the axons of bipolar cells

questions.text: Which of these is not a true muscle?
questions.explanation: The dilator pupillae is myoepithelial, derived from the pigmented epithelium of the iris, and is not a true smooth muscle, unlike the constrictor pupillae and ciliary muscles.
questions.keyConcept: The dilator pupillae is myoepithelial, not a true muscle

questions.text: Melanocytes are not present in the:
questions.explanation: The cornea is avascular and transparent and contains no melanocytes, unlike the pigmented uveal structures (iris and ciliary body) and the sclera.
questions.keyConcept: The cornea contains no melanocytes

questions.text: The most vascular part of the eye is the:
questions.explanation: The choroid, the vascular middle (uveal) coat, is the most vascular part of the eye and nourishes the outer retinal layers.
questions.keyConcept: The choroid is the most vascular part of the eye

questions.text: The outer blood-retinal barrier is made of:
questions.explanation: The outer blood-retinal barrier is formed by tight junctions between the retinal pigment epithelial cells; the inner barrier is formed by the retinal capillary endothelium.
questions.keyConcept: Outer blood-retinal barrier = tight junctions between retinal pigment epithelial cells
options: Junctional complexes between processes of Müller cells and the photoreceptors
Junctional complexes between pigmented epithelial cells

questions.text: The inner layer of the ciliary processes epithelium:
questions.explanation: The inner non-pigmented ciliary epithelium shows basal infoldings and elongated mitochondria characteristic of ion-transporting cells and secretes the aqueous humour.
questions.keyConcept: Inner ciliary epithelium is non-pigmented, has basal infoldings and secretes aqueous humour
options: Shows basal infoldings and elongated mitochondria

questions.text: The limbus is:
questions.explanation: The limbus is the corneoscleral junction; it houses the trabecular meshwork and the limbal epithelial stem cells.
questions.keyConcept: The limbus is the corneoscleral transition zone
options: The transition zone between the iris and cornea
The transition zone between the cornea and sclera
The transition zone between the iris and ciliary body

questions.text: The iridocorneal angle contains all of these structures except:
questions.explanation: The iridocorneal angle contains the canal of Schlemm, the spaces of Fontana and the pectinate ligament. Bowman's membrane is the anterior limiting layer of the cornea, not part of the angle.
questions.keyConcept: Bowman's membrane is a corneal layer, not part of the iridocorneal angle

questions.text: As regards the crista ampullaris:
questions.explanation: The crista ampullaris detects angular acceleration; its hair cells are embedded in a tall conical gelatinous cupula that lacks otoliths. Otoliths and a flat otolithic membrane belong to the maculae, and the organ of Corti is the receptor for hearing.
questions.keyConcept: The crista ampullaris has a conical cupula and no otoliths
options: It is the neuroreceptor for hearing
It is exactly similar to the macula
It has a thin glycoprotein layer

questions.text: Which of the following factors helps the cornea to be transparent?
questions.explanation: Corneal transparency depends largely on the highly regular, uniformly spaced arrangement of stromal collagen fibrils together with a relatively dehydrated stroma.
questions.keyConcept: Corneal transparency depends on the regular arrangement of stromal collagen fibers
options: Different refractive indexes of its contents

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the cornea?
questions.explanation: The cornea is kept relatively dehydrated (deturgescent) to stay transparent. It has a non-keratinized stratified epithelium, unmyelinated nerve fibers, no blood vessels and regularly arranged collagen.
questions.keyConcept: The cornea is relatively dehydrated, avascular and non-keratinized
options: It has a keratinized surface epithelium
It has irregularly arranged collagen fibers

chapters.title: Biochemistry
chapters.subtitle: Visual Cycle and Vitamin A Biochemistry

subjects.name: Biochemistry
subjects.lectures: Visual cycle and vitamin A, Deficiency of vitamin A

questions.text: Retinol is ____
questions.explanation: Retinol is the alcohol form of vitamin A (terminal CH2OH group). Retinal is the aldehyde (CHO) and retinoic acid is the carboxylic acid (COOH); the inactive provitamin A is β-carotene.
questions.keyConcept: Retinol = alcohol form of vitamin A (CH2OH)

questions.text: Preformed vitamin A (retinyl ester) is found mainly in ____
questions.explanation: Preformed vitamin A (retinyl esters) comes from animal sources and is richest in cod liver oil. Carrots, dark green vegetables and sweet potato supply provitamin A carotenoids, not preformed vitamin A.
questions.keyConcept: Preformed retinyl esters come from animal sources (cod liver)

questions.text: β-carotene is transported in blood by _______
questions.explanation: Dietary β-carotene and other carotenoids are lipophilic and are carried in the blood within lipoproteins (VLDL). Retinol-binding protein carries retinol, not carotene.
questions.keyConcept: β-carotene is carried in blood by VLDL

questions.text: Retinol is transported in blood mainly by _______
questions.explanation: Retinol is transported in plasma bound to retinol-binding protein (RBP), which circulates in a complex with transthyretin.
questions.keyConcept: Retinol is transported bound to retinol-binding protein (RBP)

questions.text: Order the following symptoms of vitamin A deficiency as it gets worse: (1) Xerophthalmia, (2) Blindness, (3) Nyctalopia, (4) Keratomalacia.
questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency progresses from nyctalopia (night blindness, 3) → xerophthalmia (1) → keratomalacia (4) → blindness (2), i.e. the order 3-1-4-2.
questions.keyConcept: Deficiency order: nyctalopia → xerophthalmia → keratomalacia → blindness

questions.text: Hypervitaminosis A causes _______
questions.explanation: Chronic vitamin A toxicity causes a range of effects including hepatomegaly, alopecia and hyperlipidemia — all of the above.
questions.keyConcept: Hypervitaminosis A: hepatomegaly, alopecia and hyperlipidemia

questions.text: Which of the following is the earliest symptom of vitamin A deficiency?
questions.explanation: Night blindness (nyctalopia) is the earliest manifestation of vitamin A deficiency, caused by impaired regeneration of rhodopsin in the rods.
questions.keyConcept: Nyctalopia (night blindness) is the earliest deficiency sign

questions.text: The antioxidant function of vitamin A is mainly by _______
questions.explanation: The antioxidant / free-radical-scavenging activity of vitamin A is attributed mainly to β-carotene.
questions.keyConcept: Antioxidant action is mainly via β-carotene

questions.text: Which of the following forms of vitamin A is used in maintenance of healthy epithelium?
questions.explanation: Per the source answer key, retinol is credited with maintaining healthy epithelial tissue (vitamin A is essential for epithelial integrity and turnover).
questions.keyConcept: Retinol maintains healthy epithelium

questions.text: Which of the following forms of vitamin A can bind to nuclear receptors and regulate the transcription of specific genes?
questions.explanation: Retinoic acid binds nuclear receptors (RAR/RXR) and acts as a transcription factor regulating expression of specific genes.
questions.keyConcept: Retinoic acid binds nuclear RAR/RXR to regulate gene transcription

questions.text: Which of the following forms of vitamin A is associated with opsin protein in the visual pigment?
questions.explanation: 11-cis retinal combines with the protein opsin to form the visual pigment rhodopsin; light isomerises it to all-trans retinal.
questions.keyConcept: 11-cis retinal binds opsin to form visual pigment (rhodopsin)

questions.text: Which one of the following is true concerning retinol?
questions.explanation: Retinol is stored in animal tissues as retinyl esters. Retinoic acid cannot be reduced back to retinol; beta-carotene (not retinol) is cleaved to yield retinal; and 11-cis-retinal is the light-absorbing chromophore of rhodopsin.
questions.keyConcept: Retinol is stored in animal tissues as retinyl esters
options: It can be formed from retinoic acid
It can be cleaved in the intestine to yield two molecules of retinal
It is the light-absorbing portion of rhodopsin
It is an inactive form of vitamin A
It is found in animal tissues as a retinyl ester

questions.text: Functions of parts of the uveal tract include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The uveal tract (vascular tunic) is made of the iris, ciliary body, and choroid. The ciliary body drives accommodation for near vision (A) and secretes the aqueous humor that fills the anterior and posterior chambers (B); the iris regulates the amount of light entering the eye (C); and the heavily pigmented choroid absorbs stray light to prevent internal reflection (D). Mechanical protection of the eye is the role of the outer fibrous tunic (cornea and sclera), not the uvea.
questions.keyConcept: Uveal tract functions: which is NOT a uveal function? -> Protection of the eye (that is the fibrous tunic).
options: Play a role in accommodation to near vision.
Secretion of fluid of anterior and posterior chambers.
Regulation of the amount of light entering eyes.
Absorption of extra light to prevent light reflection.

questions.text: The retina is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The retina is the inner nervous (sensory) tunic of the eye, NOT the vascular coat -- the vascular coat is the choroid, which belongs to the uvea, so option D is the exception. The other statements are correct: the retina is transparent (B), the fovea centralis contains only cone photoreceptors for maximal acuity (A), and the optic disc is a physiologically light-insensitive blind spot that lacks photoreceptors (C).
questions.keyConcept: Retina overview: which statement is false? -> It is the nervous coat, not the vascular coat (choroid).
options: Contains an area that contain only cones photoreceptors.
Contains a physiologically light insensitive area.
It is the vascular coat of the eyes.
Its central part is not well developed.

questions.text: Which of the following structures is correctly paired to its refractive index:
questions.explanation: The approximate refractive indices of the ocular media are: cornea about 1.38, aqueous humor about 1.33, lens about 1.40, vitreous humor about 1.34, and air = 1.00. Only the lens is paired correctly (1.4). The others are wrong: cornea is 1.38 (not 1.33), aqueous is 1.33 (not 1.34), vitreous is 1.34 (not 1.38), and air is 1.00 (not 2).
questions.keyConcept: Refractive indices: correct pairing? -> Lens approx 1.40 (cornea 1.38, aqueous 1.33, vitreous 1.34, air 1.0).

questions.text: A convex refractive lens has the ability to converge parallel light rays at a point of 25 mm distance from the lens central point. The dioptric power of this lens is:
questions.explanation: Dioptric (refractive) power in diopters equals the reciprocal of the focal length in meters: P = 1 / f. For parallel rays the convergence point is the focal point, here 25 mm = 0.025 m, so P = 1 / 0.025 = 40 D.
questions.keyConcept: Dioptric power: focal length 25 mm (0.025 m) -> P = 1/f = 40 D.

questions.text: Eye protection includes all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Protective mechanisms of the eye include the bony orbit, the lacrimal apparatus (tears flush debris and contain antibacterial lysozyme), the eyelids, and the tough outer fibrous coat. Corneal transparency is an optical property essential for vision, not a protective mechanism, so it is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Eye protection: which is NOT protective? -> Corneal transparency (an optical property, not protection).

questions.text: Functions of tears include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Tears lubricate to facilitate eyelid movement, supply oxygen for corneal nutrition, maintain a smooth uniform optical corneal surface, keep the cornea moist to preserve transparency, and provide antibacterial protection. Buffering of pH is not listed among their functions, so A is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Tear functions: which is NOT a function? -> Buffering of pH.
options: Help in maintenance of corneal transparency.

questions.text: Painless eye structures do not include:
questions.explanation: The lens, vitreous humor, choroid, and retina lack pain sensitivity. The iris, like the cornea, is richly innervated and pain-sensitive, so it does not belong among the painless structures.
questions.keyConcept: Painless eye structures: which IS pain-sensitive? -> Iris (so it is not painless).

questions.text: Regarding the cornea:
questions.explanation: The cornea is one of the most densely innervated tissues and is rich in irritant/pain receptors (C is correct). Its resting power is about 43 D (not 20), it cannot change its power for near vision, its high curvature (not low) aids strong refraction, and regulation of light entry is the job of the iris.
questions.keyConcept: Cornea: which is true? -> It contains irritant (pain) receptors.
options: It has a resting dioptric power of 20 diopters.
Increases its dioptric power in response to near vision.
Its low curvature helps in strong refraction of light.
It regulates the amount of light entering the eyes.

questions.text: Corneal transparency is due to all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Corneal transparency depends on a non-keratinized epithelium, the relative dehydration produced by the Na+ pump, the regular uniform arrangement of stromal collagen fibrils, and tight junctions limiting water entry. The degree of curvature determines refraction, not transparency, so C is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Corneal transparency: which is NOT a cause? -> High curvature (that affects refraction).
options: Na+ pump that helps osmotic suction of excess water.
Regular uniform arrangement of fibrils of substantia propria.

questions.text: Corneal transparency is due to all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Corneal transparency results from avascularity, relative dehydration (Na+ pump, plus endothelial carbonic anhydrase and Na+/H+ exchanger), and the moisturizing tear film. The cornea is in fact richly innervated, so absence of nerve supply is the false statement.
questions.keyConcept: Corneal transparency: which is false? -> Absence of nerve supply (cornea is richly innervated).
options: Absence of blood vessels in the cornea.
Absence of nerve supply to cornea.
Osmotic transport of water out secondary to the activity of Na+ pump of surface epithelium.
Carbonic anhydrase enzyme and Na+ - H+ exchanger of endothelial cells help corneal dehydration.

questions.text: Corneal nutrition occurs mainly by:
questions.explanation: Because the cornea is avascular it obtains oxygen mainly by diffusion of atmospheric oxygen dissolved in the tear film (glucose comes from the aqueous humor). Hence oxygen diffusion through tears is the main source.
questions.keyConcept: Corneal nutrition: main route? -> Oxygen diffusing through the tear film.
options: Oxygen diffusion from capillaries in the limbus.
Oxygen diffusion from iris blood vessels.

questions.text: Aqueous humor:
questions.explanation: Aqueous humor is formed largely by active secretion of the ciliary processes, a process aided by carbonic anhydrase (which is why carbonic anhydrase inhibitors lower its production). It is not secreted primarily passively, its turnover is only a few mL/day, normal intraocular pressure is about 12-20 mmHg, and corneal oxygen comes mainly from tears.
questions.keyConcept: Aqueous humor: which is true? -> Carbonic anhydrase aids its (active) formation.
options: Secreted primarily passively by ciliary processes.
Carbonic anhydrase enzyme helps in its formation.
Continuously formed and reabsorbed at a rate of 20 ml/day.
Keeps the pressure inside eyes constant at 42 mmHg.
Is the main supplier of oxygen to the cornea.

questions.text: Regarding aqueous humor, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Aqueous humor is formed actively by the non-pigmented ciliary epithelium, sets the intraocular pressure, nourishes avascular structures, and drains mainly through the trabecular meshwork at the anterior chamber angle into the canal of Schlemm -- not into the posterior chamber. Therefore C is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Aqueous humor: which is false? -> Drained in posterior chamber (it drains at the anterior chamber angle).
options: Supplies nutrients and removes metabolites from surrounding structures.
Episcleral trabecular spaces pathway represents the main mechanism of its outflow.
Formed actively by non-pigmented cells of ciliary processes.

questions.text: Which of these mechanisms is not involved in aqueous humor secretion:
questions.explanation: Aqueous secretion uses the primary active Na+/K+ ATPase, secondary active transport of glucose and amino acids, osmotic movement of water, and ion/water movement following the electrical gradient set up by Na+ transport. A HCO3-Cl- exchanger is not part of this mechanism, so D is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Aqueous secretion: which mechanism is NOT involved? -> HCO3-Cl- exchanger.
options: Secondary active transport of glucose and amino acids.

questions.text: Regarding intraocular pressure:
questions.explanation: Intraocular pressure is generated by the aqueous humor and, transmitted through the taut suspensory ligaments, helps keep the lens flattened for far vision (C). It is not produced by the vitreous, its normal range is about 12-20 mmHg, and it tends to be higher in the morning.
questions.keyConcept: Intraocular pressure: which is true? -> It exerts a flattening pressure on the lens in far vision.
options: Is the pressure caused by vitreous humor inside the eye.
Exerts flattening pressure on lens during far vision.
Keeps the suspensory ligaments stretched during near vision.
It shows diurnal variations, being higher in the evening than in the morning.

questions.text: Glaucoma:
questions.explanation: Glaucoma is a pathological rise in intraocular pressure caused mainly by obstruction to aqueous outflow -- either a closed iridocorneal angle or blocked trabecular spaces with an open angle. It is not defined by a fixed 10 mmHg rise, is rarely due to increased formation, and does not involve increased lens convexity or vitreous accumulation.
questions.keyConcept: Glaucoma: correct statement? -> Blocked iridocorneal angle or trabecular outflow raises IOP.
options: Is the increase in intraocular pressure more than 10 mmHg.
Its main cause is an increase aqueous formation.
It may be due to obstruction of iridocorneal angle or obstruction of the trabecular spaces with open iridocorneal angle.
Results in increase convexity of anterior surface of lens.
It leads to accumulation of vitreous humor.

questions.text: Regarding glaucoma, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Glaucoma is treated with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and miotics; it can damage the retina and cause blindness, impairs the ability to accommodate, and its symptoms worsen with pupillary dilatation. Atropine dilates the pupil and can precipitate angle-closure, so treated by atropine is the false statement.
questions.keyConcept: Glaucoma: which is false? -> Treated by atropine (atropine can worsen it).
options: Is treated by carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.
Results in decrease or failure of the ability of lens to change its dioptric power in near vision.
Results in pressure on retina that may lead to blindness.
Its symptoms are increased by pupillary dilatation.

questions.text: Regarding the eye lens:
questions.explanation: During accommodation the lens rounds up and increases its dioptric power to converge the diverging rays from a near object (C is correct). Its posterior surface is actually more curved than the anterior, the cornea (not the lens) provides the greatest fixed refractive power, cataract is lens opacity, and loss of lens elasticity causes presbyopia rather than blocking light.
questions.keyConcept: Eye lens: which is true? -> It increases power to focus diverging rays from near objects.
options: Its posterior surface is less curved than its anterior surface.
Is responsible for the greatest part of eye dioptric power during far vision.
Can increase its dioptric power to help refraction of diverging light coming from a near object.
In cataract, there is failure of accommodation.
Loss of its elasticity prevents passage of light through it.

questions.text: Causes of lens transparency do not include:
questions.explanation: Lens transparency depends on the regular arrangement of lens fibers, complete absence of blood vessels, high glutathione content, and osmotic balance maintained by Na+ and Ca++ pumps. The lens has no nerve supply at all, so unmyelinated nerve supply is not a valid cause.
questions.keyConcept: Lens transparency: which is NOT a cause? -> Unmyelinated nerve supply (the lens has no nerves).
options: Osmotic equilibrium by Na+ and Ca++ pumps.

questions.text: Cataract is not caused by:
questions.explanation: Cataract (lens opacity) results from ultraviolet-induced damage, denaturation of lens proteins, osmotic suction of water into the lens, and a fall in protective glutathione. Loss of lens elasticity causes presbyopia (impaired accommodation), not cataract, so E is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Cataract: which is NOT a cause? -> Decreased lens elasticity (that causes presbyopia).
options: Osmotic suction of water to the interior of the lens.

questions.text: Near response includes all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The near response comprises convergence of both eyes (medial recti), accommodation (ciliary contraction with relaxed zonules), and pupillary constriction/miosis via the constrictor pupillae, all driven by the oculomotor nerve with cortical input. Contraction of the dilator pupillae would cause mydriasis, the opposite, so D is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Near response: which is NOT part of it? -> Contraction of dilator pupillae (near response causes miosis).
options: Stimulation of somatic and autonomic fibers of oculomotor nerve.
Contraction of ciliary muscle and relaxation of suspensory ligaments.
Contraction of dilator papillae muscles of both eyes.
Stimulation of the superior colliculus by areas 18 & 19.

questions.text: In near response:
questions.explanation: In the near response the ciliary muscle contracts, the suspensory ligaments relax, and the lens (especially its anterior surface) becomes more convex, increasing its dioptric power (D). Miosis aids focusing on the central lens, convergence keeps images on corresponding retinal points, ciliary contraction relaxes (not stretches) the zonules, and the cerebral cortex, not the pretectum, drives accommodation.
questions.keyConcept: Near response: which is true? -> Increased convexity and power of the lens anterior surface.
options: The importance of miosis is to help in focusing of image of near object on 2 corresponding parts of retina.
Medial convergence helps to prevent falling of light on peripheral parts of lens.
Contraction of ciliary muscle leads to stretch of suspensory ligaments.
Increase convexity and dioptric power of anterior surface of lens.
Pretectal area of midbrain stimulates EW nucleus.

questions.text: Accommodation reflex:
questions.explanation: Glaucoma impairs the ciliary apparatus and the ability of the lens to change its power, so the accommodation reflex is lost (C). It is unrelated to lens transparency, decreases (not increases) with reduced lens elasticity, operates on near objects, and increases lens (not corneal) power.
questions.keyConcept: Accommodation reflex: which is true? -> It is lost in glaucoma.
options: Decreases by decrease in lens transparency.
Occurs when objects are at a distance of 6 meters and more from eyes.
Associated with an increase in dioptric power of anterior surface of cornea.

questions.text: The center of accommodation reflex is:
questions.explanation: In this course the center coordinating the accommodation reflex is the superior colliculus, which relays cortical signals (areas 17-19) to the Edinger-Westphal and oculomotor nuclei. The pretectal area is the center for the light reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Accommodation reflex center: -> Superior colliculus.

questions.text: The following is a part of accommodation reflex:
questions.explanation: During accommodation for near objects the ciliary muscle contracts and relaxes the suspensory ligaments, decreasing the pull on the lens capsule so the lens rounds up (E). The other options describe relaxation/far vision or wrongly attribute the curvature change to the cornea.
questions.keyConcept: Accommodation reflex component: -> Decreased pull on the lens capsule (zonules relax).
options: Optical changes in response to shifting vision to a far object.
Light rays entering the eyes become parallel.
Decrease pull on the lens capsule.

questions.text: Purkinje- Sanson image is:
questions.explanation: The Purkinje-Sanson images are reflections from the corneal and lens surfaces; the change in the image reflected from the anterior lens surface during accommodation proves that this surface increases its convexity. It is not related to dark adaptation, cataract, chiasmal lesions, or myopia.
questions.keyConcept: Purkinje-Sanson image: -> Evidence of increased lens anterior-surface convexity during accommodation.
options: A shift from day-light vision to night vision.
A prove of increase convexity of anterior surface of lens.
An unclear vision occurs with cataract.
A disturbed vision due to lesion in the optic chiasma.
An error of refraction associated with myopia.

questions.text: Range of accommodation is the:
questions.explanation: The range of accommodation is the linear distance between the far point and the near point -- the interval over which objects can be seen clearly. The difference between maximal and minimal lens power is instead the amplitude (power) of accommodation.
questions.keyConcept: Range of accommodation: -> The distance between the far point and the near point.
options: Nearest point to the eye at which objects are seen clearly.
Far point from the eye at which objects are seen clearly.
Difference between maximal lens power and minimal lens power.
Difference between far point and near point.
The power of the lens on looking at a near object.

questions.text: Which of the following occurs during normal near response:
questions.explanation: During the normal near response both eyes converge (medial recti), the lens (not the cornea) increases its curvature, miosis reduces spherical and chromatic aberrations, and images fall on corresponding retinal points. Hence convergence (A) is the correct event.
questions.keyConcept: Normal near response: -> Both eyes converge.
options: Falling of light from near object on non-corresponding retinal points.
Decrease curvature of posterior lens surface.

questions.text: The refractive index of the cornea is:
questions.explanation: The cornea has a refractive index of approximately 1.38 (aqueous and vitreous about 1.33-1.34, lens about 1.40, air = 1.0).
questions.keyConcept: Refractive index of the cornea: -> 1.38.

questions.text: When parallel light strikes a convex lens, the area of focusing of light behind the lens is the:
questions.explanation: Parallel light striking a convex lens converges to the focal point behind the lens; the distance from the lens to that point is the focal length. The nodal point, dioptric power, and object distance are different optical quantities.
questions.keyConcept: Convex lens and parallel rays: -> They converge at the focal point.

questions.text: According to lens formula, any change in object distance is associated with a change in:
questions.explanation: In the eye the image distance is fixed (the retina lies at a constant distance), so by the lens relationship any change in object distance must be compensated by a change in the lens dioptric power (accommodation). Hence B.
questions.keyConcept: Lens formula in the eye: changing object distance changes -> lens dioptric power.

questions.text: Which of the following is an anatomical eye protective mechanism:
questions.explanation: Among the options, the eyelid is the anatomical (structural) protective mechanism. The tear film is a secretory mechanism, and the various eye-closure responses are protective reflexes rather than anatomical structures.
questions.keyConcept: Anatomical eye protective mechanism: -> The eyelid (the others are protective reflexes).
options: Eye closure in response to loud sound.
Eye closure in response to conjunctival irritation.
Eye closure in response to moving objects close to eyes.

questions.text: Reflex tear secretion is NOT:
questions.explanation: Reflex tear secretion is evoked by stimuli such as corneal or conjunctival irritation, with the trigeminal nerve (V) as afferent and the facial nerve (VII) as efferent. Continuous baseline tearing is basal secretion, not reflex, so A does not describe reflex secretion.
questions.keyConcept: Reflex tear secretion: which is NOT true of it? -> Continuous throughout the day (that is basal secretion).
options: Its afferent is the V cranial nerve.
Its efferent is the VII cranial nerve.
Occurs in response to corneal irritation.

questions.text: Decrees secretion of tear occurs in:
questions.explanation: Reduced tear secretion occurs in xerosis (dry-eye conditions). Psychic states, strong emotions, and corneal irritation increase tearing, and basal secretion is continuous, so the only condition with decreased secretion is xerosis.
questions.keyConcept: Decreased tear secretion: occurs in -> xerosis (dry eye).

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause for corneal transparency:
questions.explanation: Corneal transparency is due to the tear film, avascularity, the Na+/K+ pumps of the epithelium and endothelium, and corneal dehydration. The cornea is richly innervated, so absence of nerve supply is not a cause of transparency.
questions.keyConcept: Corneal transparency: which is NOT a cause? -> Absence of nerve supply (cornea is innervated).
options: Na+-K+ pump of surface epithelial and of endothelial cells.

questions.text: The main mechanism involved in aquous humor formation is:
questions.explanation: Aqueous humor is formed mainly by a primary active mechanism (Na+/K+ ATPase of the ciliary epithelium), with secondary active transport, osmosis, filtration, and diffusion playing minor roles. Hence the primary active mechanism predominates.
questions.keyConcept: Aqueous humor formation: main mechanism -> primary active secretion.

questions.text: The part of the crystalline lens that maintains its vitality is the:
questions.explanation: The metabolically active anterior lens epithelium maintains the lens vitality through its ion pumps, metabolism, and production of new fibers. The capsule, equator, and zonules are not metabolic, and the avascular lens has no blood vessels.
questions.keyConcept: Lens vitality maintained by: -> the lens epithelium.

questions.text: The increase in lens diopteric power during near vision is performed by:
questions.explanation: For near vision the ciliary muscle contracts, which relaxes the suspensory ligaments (zonules); the lens capsule then molds the lens into a more convex, higher-power shape. Therefore relaxation of the suspensory ligaments increases lens power.
questions.keyConcept: Increasing lens power for near vision: -> relaxation of the suspensory ligaments.
options: Increase convexity of lens posterior surface.

questions.text: In near response, miosis helps in:
questions.explanation: Miosis in the near response restricts light to the central, most powerful, and optically regular part of the lens, reducing spherical and chromatic aberrations. It does not direct light to peripheral lens parts.
questions.keyConcept: Miosis in near response helps: -> light falls on the central (most powerful) part of the lens.
options: Focusing of divergent light on the reina.
Falling of image of object on corresponding retinal areas.
Falling of light on the most powerful part of the lens.
Falling of light on the peripheral lens parts.
Falling of light on the prism-like part of the lens.

questions.text: In young healthy adults, the maximally accommodating lens power is:
questions.explanation: At rest the lens contributes about 20 D; with maximal accommodation a young adult can add roughly 14 D, giving a maximally accommodating lens power of about 34 D.
questions.keyConcept: Young adult maximal accommodating lens power: -> about 34 D.

questions.text: The lens formula reflects that:
questions.explanation: Because the image distance in the eye is fixed (the retina), the lens formula implies the lens must change its dioptric power as the object distance changes -- the basis of accommodation. So C is correct.
questions.keyConcept: Lens formula (eye): -> lens power changes as object distance changes (image distance fixed).
options: The lens diopteric power changes as the object distance changes.
The image distance is the distance from the object to the retina.
The image distance changes as the object distance changes.

questions.text: Most of light refraction occurs at:
questions.explanation: The largest jump in refractive index along the visual axis is from air (1.0) to cornea (about 1.38), so most refraction of light occurs at the air-corneal interface rather than at the internal interfaces.
questions.keyConcept: Greatest light refraction occurs at: -> the air-cornea interface.

questions.text: Normal Intraocular pressure is characterized by:
questions.explanation: Normal intraocular pressure is set by the balance of aqueous formation and outflow, with outflow through the trabecular meshwork being the principal regulated factor. It depends on aqueous (not vitreous), its normal range is about 12-20 mmHg, and it tends to be higher in the morning.
questions.keyConcept: Normal intraocular pressure: -> mainly regulated by the rate of aqueous outflow.
options: Depends on the amount of vitreous.
Is normally higher at the evening than in the morning.
Is mainly regulated by rate of aqueous outflow.
It prevents any change in lens curvature.

questions.text: Glaucoma may be treated by:
questions.explanation: Parasympathomimetics (miotics such as pilocarpine) cause miosis and ciliary contraction that open the iridocorneal angle and improve aqueous outflow, lowering intraocular pressure. Pupil-dilators and atropine-like or sympathomimetic agents tend to worsen angle-closure glaucoma.
questions.keyConcept: Glaucoma treatment: -> parasympathomimetics (miotics) that improve outflow.

questions.text: Increase in lens diopteric power, than its resting power, is:
questions.explanation: Lens power rises above its resting level during accommodation for near vision, mediated by parasympathetic-driven ciliary muscle contraction that relaxes the zonules and increases the curvature (convexity) of the anterior lens surface (E). It is for near (not far) vision and is not produced by sympathetic stimulation or by stretching of the suspensory ligaments.
questions.keyConcept: Increasing lens power above resting: -> increased curvature of its anterior surface.
options: Occurs by stimulation of sympathetic nerves of the eye.
Is mediated by relaxation of ciliary muscle.
Is facilitated by stretching of the suspensory ligaments.
Occurs by increase in its anterior surface curvature.

questions.text: Regarding refraction of light rays in the eyes, all of the following sentences are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: In emmetropia parallel rays from a distant object focus on the retina with the lens at rest, i.e. with ZERO accommodation, so statement A is the false exception. The rest are true: maximal accommodation occurs at the near point, zero at the far point, and both the power and range of accommodation decline with age.
questions.keyConcept: Emmetropia: focuses parallel rays on the retina at rest (zero accommodation), not maximal.
options: Emmetropic eye can focus parallel light rays on retina with maximal accommodation.
At near point, there is maximal accommodation.
At far point, there is zero accommodation.
Power of accommodation decreases by age.
Range of accommodation decreases by age.

questions.text: Regarding errors of refraction:
questions.explanation: Keratoconus increases corneal curvature and refractive power and therefore causes myopia (B is correct). Presbyopia is loss of lens elasticity (not increased power), ciliary spasm causes myopia (not hypermetropia), astigmatism is from unequal curvature (not aphakia), and accommodative squint is linked to hypermetropia.
questions.keyConcept: Keratoconus increases corneal curvature/power, producing myopia.
options: Presbyopia occurs due to increase dioptric power of cornea or lens.
Spasm of ciliary muscle results in hypermetropia.
Myopic children are likely to develop squint.

questions.text: In errors of refraction:
questions.explanation: Loss of accommodation in presbyopia pushes the near point farther from the eye, so A is correct. Myopia is corrected by a concave (not convex) lens, the near point is farther (not closer) in hypermetropia, astigmatism affects both points, and it is a pathological (not physiological) error.
questions.keyConcept: Presbyopia: the near point recedes away from the eye.
options: Near point recedes away from eyes in presbyopia.
Increase eye power by a convex lens is the treatment of myopia.
Near point is closer to eyes in hypermetropia.
Astigmatism affects near point more than far point.
Astigmatism is a physiological error of refraction.

questions.text: In errors of refraction, all of the following sentences are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The near point does change in refractive errors (it recedes in hypermetropia and presbyopia), so D is the false exception. In myopia the far point comes nearer, in hypermetropia the far point is reached only by accommodating, in presbyopia the far point is unchanged, and the near point lengthens in presbyopia.
questions.keyConcept: The near point is NOT unchanged in all errors -- it shifts in hypermetropia and presbyopia.
options: Far point becomes near than normal in myopia.
Far point remains normal, but with the use of accommodation in hypermetropia.
Far point is unchanged in presbyopia.
Near point is unchanged in all errors of refraction.
Near point distance is longer than normal in presbyopia

questions.text: In refraction errors:
questions.explanation: Hypermetropia is corrected with a converging (convex) lens, so C is correct. Presbyopia needs a convex (not biconcave) lens, myopia a concave (not biconvex) lens, astigmatism a cylindrical (not diverging) lens, and not all errors are corrected by a sphero-cylindrical lens.
questions.keyConcept: Hypermetropia is corrected by a converging (convex) lens.
options: Presbyopia is corrected by a biconcave lens.
Myopia is corrected by a biconvex lens.
Hypermetropia is corrected by a converging lens.
Astigmatism is corrected by diverging lens.
All errors of refraction are corrected by sphero-cylindrical lens

questions.text: In presbyopia:
questions.explanation: Presbyopia is the age-related loss of lens elasticity that progressively reduces the power and range of accommodation (D). It is not loss of transparency, the far point is unchanged, the near point recedes (gets farther), and it is corrected by a convex lens for near vision.
questions.keyConcept: Presbyopia: power and range of accommodation progressively decrease.
options: Occurs due to loss of lens transparency.
The far point gets closer to the eyes.
The near point gets closer to the eyes.
The power and range of accommodation are progressively decreased.
Corrected by convex lens to help far and near vision.

questions.text: In myopia:
questions.explanation: Myopia can result from an abnormally high corneal curvature (refractive type) or an elongated globe, so C is correct. Rays focus in front of the retina, axial length is increased (not decreased), the far point comes nearer, and the near point comes closer.
questions.keyConcept: Myopia may be due to higher-than-normal corneal curvature (or a long eyeball).
options: Parallel light rays are focused behind the retina.
May be due to axial decrease in eye ball length.
May be due to high than normal corneal curvature.
The punctum proximum is increased than normal.

questions.text: In hypermetropia:
questions.explanation: In hypermetropia the near point (punctum proximum) is farther than normal, so B is correct. The far point is virtual/behind the eye, lens power is not increased, it occurs in a short (not keratoconic) eye, and it is treated by a convex (not concave) lens.
questions.keyConcept: Hypermetropia: the near point (punctum proximum) is farther than normal.
options: Punctum remotum is less than normal.
Punctum proximum is more than normal.
The power of the lens is markedly increased.

questions.text: Regarding hyperopia:
questions.explanation: Hyperopes accommodate even for distance, and this excessive accommodation and convergence cause headache and accommodative squint in children (C). They see far better than near, are corrected by a converging lens, rays focus behind the retina, and the eyeball is short (not long).
questions.keyConcept: Hyperopia: excess accommodation causes headache and accommodative squint in children.
options: Can see near objects better than far objects.
Excessive accommodation of the patient can produce headache and squint in children.
Parallel light rays are focused in front of retina.
Has an eye ball of long size.

questions.text: Regarding the iris:
questions.explanation: The iris regulates light entry by changing pupil size (C). It is not a refractive medium, constriction (not dilation) reduces aberrations, the constrictor tone normally dominates, and its main role is light regulation rather than protection.
questions.keyConcept: Iris regulates the amount of light entering the eye.
options: It is one of the refractive eye media.
Dilatation of its pupil prevents chromatic and spherical aberrations.
Has a dominant tone of dilator pupillae over constrictor pupillae muscle.
Its function is mainly to protect the underlying structures.

questions.text: In Light reflex, all of the following sentences are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The indirect (consensual) light reflex is due to the pretectal area projecting bilaterally to both Edinger-Westphal nuclei, not to the lateral geniculate body, so C is the false exception. The reflex localizes pathway lesions, constricts both pupils, is lost with preserved near response in tabes dorsalis, and activates both oculomotor parasympathetic outflows.
questions.keyConcept: Consensual light reflex: pretectal area projects to BOTH EW nuclei, not to the LGB.
options: Can be used for diagnosis and localization of lesions in visual pathway.
It involves constriction of pupil of both eyes in response to light exposure of one eye.
Its indirect component is due to bilateral stimulation of lateral geniculate body by pretectal area.
It is lost without loss of near response in case of tabes dorsalis.
During which, parasympathetic fibers of both oculomotor nerves are activated.

questions.text: All of the following produce miosis EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Parasympatholytic (anticholinergic) drugs such as atropine block the constrictor pupillae and cause mydriasis, so D is the exception. Deep (3rd-stage) anesthesia, Horner syndrome, pretectal-to-EWN drive, and sleep all cause miosis.
questions.keyConcept: Parasympatholytics cause mydriasis, NOT miosis.
options: Impulses from pretectal area and superior colliculus to EWN.

questions.text: All of the following produce mydriasis EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Opioids such as morphine cause miosis (pinpoint pupils), so B is the exception. Light (2nd-stage) anesthesia, stress and emotion, far vision, and atropine all cause mydriasis.
questions.keyConcept: Morphine causes miosis (pinpoint pupils), NOT mydriasis.

questions.text: All of the following statements are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: An amaurotic pupil (blind eye from an optic nerve lesion) shows no direct light reflex on the affected side, so A is the false exception. Light-near dissociation is from pretectal lesions, a hemianopic pupil reacts when light enters the seeing field, a fixed dilated pupil is a sign of death, and dark vision causes mydriasis.
questions.keyConcept: Amaurotic pupil: the blind eye has NO direct light reflex.
options: Amauratic pupil gives normal direct light reflex.
Light-near dissociation occurs due to lesion in pretectal area of midbrain.
Hemianopic pupil gives normal bilateral light reflex when light falls from the normal half of the visual field.
Dilated irreactive pupil is a diagnostic sign of death.

questions.text: Concerning the retina:
questions.explanation: The first-order (bipolar) and second-order (ganglion) neurons of the visual pathway lie inside the retina, so B is correct. Rods and cones are nourished by the choroid (not retinal vessels), ganglion cells are driven by bipolar (not horizontal) cells, the pigment epithelium contacts the choroid (not vitreous), and horizontal (not Muller) cells give lateral inhibition.
questions.keyConcept: Retina: the 1st and 2nd order neurons (bipolar, ganglion) lie within the retina.
options: Rods and cones receive their blood supply from retinal blood vessels.
The 1st and the 2nd order neurons of visual pathway lie inside the retina.
Ganglion cells are stimulated by bipolar and horizontal cells.
Pigment epithelial cell layer is in direct contact to vitreous humor.
Muller cells produce lateral inhibition that helps in sharpening of vision.

questions.text: Visual acuity is maximal at fovea centralis due to all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The fovea contains only cones (no rods), so attributing its acuity to a 1:1 rod-and-cone-to-bipolar ratio is incorrect -- C is the exception. High acuity comes from 1:1 cone-to-bipolar-to-ganglion connection (no convergence), absence of overlying vessels, and the xanthophyll pigment, and its cones are low-sensitivity high-threshold receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Foveal acuity: the fovea has only cones (no rods), so a 1:1 rod-and-cone ratio is wrong.
options: Visual receptors in fovea are only low sensitivity, high threshold receptors.
In the fovea, no convergence of impulses.
Rods and cones of fovea are connected to bipolar cells in 1:1 ratio.
Photoreceptors in this area are not covered by blood vessels.

questions.text: The retinal bipolar cells:
questions.explanation: Bipolar cells are the first-order neuron of the visual pathway (D). They are not the photoreceptors, do not discharge continuously, are excited directly by photoreceptors (not via horizontal cells), and the parvo/magno classification belongs to ganglion cells.
questions.keyConcept: Bipolar cells are the 1st-order neuron of the visual pathway.
options: Are the photo-sensitive receptors of retina.
Continuously discharge impulses even when unstimulated.
Are indirectly excited and depolarized by rods and cones through the horizontal cells.
Represent the 1st order neuron of the visual pathway.
Are of 2 types; parvo and magno cells.

questions.text: The horizontal cells of the retina:
questions.explanation: Horizontal cells produce lateral inhibition of weakly stimulated neighboring pathways, sharpening contrast and edges (E). They do not relay bipolar-to-ganglion signals, their output is inhibitory (not excitatory glutamate), they are not photosensitive, and they are not the 2nd-order neuron.
questions.keyConcept: Horizontal cells produce lateral inhibition that sharpens contrast and boundaries.
options: Transmit impulses from bipolar cells to ganglion cells.
Have excitatory output through release of glutamate neurotransmitter.
Very sensitive to photon of light.
Represent the 2nd order neuron in the visual pathway.
Produce lateral inhibition of near-by weakly stimulated pathways to clarify contrast and boundaries.

questions.text: The amacrine cells of retina:
questions.explanation: Amacrine cells participate in processing and analysis of visual signals such as motion and transient responses (B). They do not carry photoreceptor-to-bipolar impulses, lateral inhibition is by horizontal cells, they are not the 1st-order neuron, and ganglion (not amacrine) axons form the optic nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Amacrine cells help analyze visual signals (e.g., motion).
options: Carry impulses from photoreceptors to bipolar cells.
Help in analysis of visual signals.
Responsible for lateral inhibition of near-by weakly stimulated visual pathways.
Are the 1st order neuron of visual pathway.
Their axons form the optic nerve.

questions.text: Muller cells of retina share in the following functions EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor outer-segment discs is a function of the retinal pigment epithelium, not Muller cells, so D is the exception. Muller cells form the limiting membranes, store glycogen, remove debris, and take up neurotransmitters.
questions.keyConcept: Phagocytosis of shed photoreceptor discs is by the pigment epithelium, not Muller cells.
options: Formation of limiting membranes for support of retina.

questions.text: Retinal ganglion cells:
questions.explanation: Retinal ganglion cells discharge action potentials continuously, including in the dark, with light modulating their firing rate (C). They are the 2nd-order (not 1st-order) neuron, receive bipolar (direct) and amacrine input, are classed as parvo/magno, and fire all-or-none action potentials (not just local hyperpolarization).
questions.keyConcept: Ganglion cells fire continuously, even in the dark; light modulates the rate.
options: Are the 1st order neuron in the visual pathway.
Receive impulses from photoreceptors directly, and from amacrine cells indirectly.
Continuously transmit impulses even during dark.
Are of 2 types, depolarizing and hyperpolarizing.
Respond by generating a hyperpolarization local potential changes.

questions.text: Parvoganglion cells of retina are:
questions.explanation: Parvocellular (P) ganglion cells are small and slowly conducting with small receptive fields and are color-specific, mediating fine detail and color (E). Rapid conduction, large size, large fields, and motion/intensity detection describe magnocellular cells.
questions.keyConcept: Parvocellular ganglion cells are color-specific (small, slow, small fields).

questions.text: Magnoganglion cells of retina are:
questions.explanation: Magnocellular (M) ganglion cells are large and fast-conducting with large receptive fields and detect movement (D). Small size, small fields, color projection, and edge/detail perception are parvocellular features.
questions.keyConcept: Magnocellular ganglion cells detect movement (large, fast, large fields).
options: Receive impulses from a small area in the retina.
Project to color sensitive neurons in lateral geniculate body.
Detect movement of objects in the visual field.
Responsible for perception of edges and details of objects.

questions.text: Receptive field of retina is:
questions.explanation: The receptive field is the retinal area whose photoreceptors converge onto a specific bipolar and ganglion cell (A). It is not the area of sharpest vision, the blind spot, the vessel entry point, or a rod-only zone.
questions.keyConcept: Receptive field: retinal area that feeds a specific bipolar and ganglion cell.
options: An area that send impulses to specific bipolar and ganglion cells.
An area with insensitivity to light.
An area where retinal vessels enter the eyes.
An area that contains only rods.

questions.text: Optic disc is NOT characterized by:
questions.explanation: In glaucoma the optic-disc cup is enlarged and deepened (cupping), not obliterated -- obliteration of the cup occurs in papilledema -- so E does not characterize the disc. It is normally a blind spot, has a physiological cup, is where all retinal layers end except ganglion axons, and swells with raised intracranial pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Optic disc cup is exaggerated (not obliterated) in glaucoma; obliteration is papilledema.
options: All retinal layers end except axons of ganglion cells.
Becomes edematous if the intracranial pressure is very high.
Its cup is obliterated in glaucoma.

questions.text: Xanthophyll pigments of macula lutea do NOT help in:
questions.explanation: Generating photoreceptor potential changes is the role of the visual pigments (rhodopsin/iodopsin), not the xanthophyll macular pigment, so A is the exception. Xanthophyll absorbs excess light, prevents reflection, acts as an antioxidant, and filters ultraviolet rays.
questions.keyConcept: Xanthophyll macular pigment does NOT generate photoreceptor potentials.
options: Generate potential changes in photoreceptors on light exposure.
Absorption of extra light reaching the retina.

questions.text: Macular degeneration is:
questions.explanation: In macular degeneration the central macular cones are lost while the peripheral retina (rods, high light sensitivity) remains intact (B). It is not glaucoma-induced, central vision is lost (not preserved), it affects cones (not spares them), and color perception is impaired.
questions.keyConcept: Macular degeneration spares the peripheral retina (rods, high sensitivity).
options: Associated with intact areas of retina with high light sensitivity.
A disease that affect rods but not cones.
Associated with no effect on color perception.

questions.text: In the fovea of the retina:
questions.explanation: The fovea contains only cones, which have low light sensitivity and a high threshold, so it is less sensitive to light (C). Its cones are slender (not large), convergence is minimal (1:1), the threshold is high (not low), and it serves photopic (not scotopic) vision.
questions.keyConcept: Fovea is less sensitive to light (cones: low sensitivity, high threshold).
options: The photoreceptors are only large cones.
Receptors output shows a high degree of convergence.
There is less sensitivity to light.
The threshold needed for receptor stimulation is low.
Scotopic vision is its main function.

questions.text: In the whole retina, except the fovea:
questions.explanation: Outside the fovea the photoreceptors are predominantly rods (A). The peripheral connection ratio shows high convergence (many-to-one, not 1:1), the threshold is low (high sensitivity), colors and details are poorly perceived, and sharpest vision is a foveal function.
questions.keyConcept: Outside the fovea photoreceptors are mainly rods.
options: The photoreceptors to bipolar cells to ganglion cells connection ratio is one to one.
The threshold of stimulation of photoreceptors is high.
Colors and details are perceived accurately.
Sharpest vision is its main function.

questions.text: Rods differ from cones in that they are of:
questions.explanation: Rods provide low visual acuity compared with cones (D). Rods are far more numerous (not fewer), have a low threshold and high sensitivity (not high threshold/low sensitivity), and both rods and cones contain photosensitive pigments, so that is not distinguishing.
questions.keyConcept: Rods differ from cones in giving low visual acuity.

questions.text: Cones differ from rods in that they are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Cones contain iodopsin (photopsin) pigments (C). They have high (not low) color perception, mediate photopic (not scotopic) vision, show low convergence (1:1), and are less light-sensitive than rods.
questions.keyConcept: Cones contain iodopsin (photopsin) pigment.

questions.text: Scotopic vision differs from photopic vision in:
questions.explanation: In scotopic (rod) vision the spectral sensitivity peak is around 505 nm (B). Scotopic vision is peripheral (not central), colors are not perceived, it has a low threshold (high sensitivity), and it is a rod (not cone) function.
questions.keyConcept: Scotopic vision peaks near 505 nm (Purkinje shift to blue).
options: The most luminous is the 505 nm wave length of the spectrum.
All colors of the spectrum are perceived clearly.
It is high threshold of stimulation type of vision.
It is the function of cones

questions.text: Photopic vision is NOT characterized by being:
questions.explanation: Photopic (cone) vision has a high threshold of stimulation (low sensitivity), so calling it low-threshold is wrong -- E is the exception. It is correctly daylight vision, cone vision, low light-sensitivity, and high acuity.
questions.keyConcept: Photopic vision has a HIGH threshold (low sensitivity), not low threshold.

questions.text: Vitamin A deficiency leads to all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Vitamin A deficiency does not make the iris red, so C is the exception. It causes night blindness (nyctalopia), degeneration of cones and of the neural retinal layers, and impaired dark adaptation.
questions.keyConcept: Vitamin A deficiency does NOT turn the iris red.
options: Degeneration of neural layers of retina.

questions.text: Light-dependent photochemical changes in the retina include:
questions.explanation: Light isomerizes 11-cis retinal into all-trans retinal, the primary photochemical event that activates rhodopsin (A). The other listed conversions are regeneration (visual cycle) steps occurring in the dark or are stated incorrectly.
questions.keyConcept: Light isomerizes 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal.
options: Conversion of 11-cis retinal into all-trans retinal.
Conversion of all-trans reinal into all-trans retinol.
Conversion of all-trans retinol into 11-cis retinol.
Conversion of 11-cis retinal from a straight into a curved configuration.

questions.text: During phototransduction in response to light:
questions.explanation: In light, cGMP-gated Na+ channels close and the photoreceptor hyperpolarizes, so its membrane potential becomes more negative (D). Na+ influx falls (not rises), cGMP breakdown closes channels (not pumps), glutamate release decreases, and the outer (not inner) segment pigment is bleached.
questions.keyConcept: Phototransduction: the photoreceptor hyperpolarizes (more negative) in light.
options: Increased Na+ influx depolarizes visual receptors.
Breakdown of cGMP leads to closure of Na+ pumps.
Glutamate released from receptors directly excites bipolar cells.
Receptor membrane potential shifts to a more negative value.
The photosensitive pigments in the inner segment of photoreceptor become bleached.

questions.text: The main part of the photoreceptor that mediate the electrical changes during light exposure is:
questions.explanation: The electrical response to light is mediated by the cGMP-gated Na+ channels in the OUTER segment, which close when cGMP falls (B). The Na+ pumps and inner-segment channels are not the light-sensitive elements.
questions.keyConcept: Light response is mediated by cGMP-gated Na+ channels in the outer segment.
options: Na+ cotransport carrier in outer segment.

questions.text: Which of the following is a key step in breakdown of cGMP of Na+ channels in photoreceptors:
questions.explanation: Activated rhodopsin stimulates the G-protein transducin, which activates phosphodiesterase to break down cGMP and close Na+ channels (C). Guanylyl cyclase synthesizes (not degrades) cGMP, and rhodopsin, rhodopsin kinase, and glutamate are not the direct hydrolysis step.
questions.keyConcept: Transducin links activated rhodopsin to cGMP breakdown.

questions.text: The only cell in the retina that responds by all or none response is:
questions.explanation: Only retinal ganglion cells generate all-or-none action potentials; photoreceptors, bipolar, horizontal, and amacrine cells respond with graded local potentials (C).
questions.keyConcept: Only ganglion cells generate all-or-none action potentials in the retina.

questions.text: During dark adaptation:
questions.explanation: During dark adaptation rhodopsin and cone pigments are regenerated, so photosensitive pigment concentration rises (A). The pupil dilates (not constricts), rods ultimately reach far higher sensitivity than cones, retinal sensitivity increases (not decreases), and the scotopic peak is about 505 nm (not 550).
questions.keyConcept: Dark adaptation: photosensitive pigment concentration increases.
options: The concentration of receptor photosensitive pigments is increased.
Pigments in rods are more rapidly regenerated than pigments in cones.
The sensitivity of retina is decreased.
Maximal luminicity occurs to wave length 550 nm.

questions.text: During light adaptation:
questions.explanation: In light adaptation pigments are bleached so retinal sensitivity falls and the threshold rises (B). The pupil constricts (not dilates maximally), sensitivity decreases, bleaching exceeds regeneration, and the photopic peak is about 555 nm (yellow-green), not blue-green.
questions.keyConcept: Light adaptation: retinal threshold increases (sensitivity falls).
options: Regeneration of pigments is more than bleaching.
The most luminous spectral color is the green-blue

questions.text: The type of astigmatism when 2 meridians are ammetropoic of the same type is:
questions.explanation: When both principal meridians have the same type of ametropia (both myopic or both hyperopic) but of different degrees, it is compound regular astigmatism (B). Simple has one emmetropic meridian, mixed has one myopic and one hyperopic meridian, and irregular has uneven meridians.
questions.keyConcept: Compound regular astigmatism: both meridians ametropic of the same type.

questions.text: Pupil constriction conditions help in:
questions.explanation: Pupillary constriction increases the depth of focus and reduces spherical and chromatic aberrations (D). The other options are aberrations it reduces (rather than promotes) or are unrelated.
questions.keyConcept: Pupil constriction increases depth of focus (and cuts aberrations).
options: Diagnosis of lesions in the visual cortex.

questions.text: The depth of focus is:
questions.explanation: Depth of focus is inversely related to pupil size -- a smaller pupil gives greater depth of focus (E). Mydriatic conditions (adrenaline, atropine, light anesthesia) reduce it, and it is not set simply by viewing distance.
questions.keyConcept: Depth of focus is inversely related to pupil size.
options: Increases during the 2nd stage of anesthesia.
Increases by focusing on far, but not on near objects.
Inversely related to the pupil size.

questions.text: Nervous pathway of pupillary light reflex DOES NOT involve:
questions.explanation: The pupillary light reflex leaves the optic tract before the lateral geniculate body and bypasses the optic radiations and cortex, so optic radiations are not involved (D). It does use the optic nerve, anterior optic tract fibers, the pretectal area, and the oculomotor nerve.
questions.keyConcept: Pupillary light reflex does NOT involve the optic radiations.

questions.text: The retinal horizontal cells are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Horizontal cells mediate lateral inhibition that sharpens focus and enhances contrast (E). They are not the 2nd-order neuron, do not release excitatory glutamate onto bipolar cells, and do not converge bipolar-to-ganglion signals.
questions.keyConcept: Horizontal cells: lateral inhibition that aids focusing and contrast.
options: Being the 2nd order neuron of the visual pathway.
Converge impulses from bipolar cells to ganglion cells.
Responsible for lateral inhibition to help focusing and contrast.

questions.text: Papilledema is a term to describe:
questions.explanation: Papilledema, from raised intracranial pressure, swells the disc and obliterates the physiological cup (B). Exaggerated cupping occurs in glaucoma, and disc pallor describes optic atrophy.
questions.keyConcept: Papilledema: swelling that obliterates the optic-disc cup.
options: Obliteration of cupping of optic disc.

questions.text: Cones in the fovea are unique than other retinal cones in having:
questions.explanation: Foveal cones are unique in having a 1:1 connection to bipolar and ganglion cells with little or no convergence, giving the highest acuity (C). Low sensitivity, high threshold, color detection, and daylight vision are shared by all cones.
questions.keyConcept: Foveal cones are unique in 1:1 connection with little/no convergence.
options: 1: 1 connection, with no or little convergence.

questions.text: During dark, photoreceptors are:
questions.explanation: In the dark, cGMP keeps Na+ channels open so the photoreceptor is partially depolarized (the dark current) and continuously releases glutamate (A). It is not hyperpolarized, releases glutamate (not GABA), has open (not closed) outer-segment Na+ channels, and regenerates (not decomposes) pigment.
questions.keyConcept: In the dark, photoreceptors are partially depolarized (dark current).
options: Release GABA to inhibit bipolar cells.
Have a closed Na+ channels in their outer segment.

questions.text: In dark adaptation of the retina:
questions.explanation: During dark adaptation retinal sensitivity rises so the neural signal intensity increases (D). Pigment concentration increases (not decreases), sensitivity becomes high (not low), the pupil dilates (not constricts), and peak sensitivity is about 505 nm (not 550).
questions.keyConcept: Dark adaptation: signal intensity in retinal neurons increases.
options: The concentration of photochemical substances is decreasing.
The signal intensity in retinal neurons is increased.
The retina is most sensitive to light of wavelength 550 nm.

questions.text: Cortical visual areas:
questions.explanation: The primary visual cortex (area 17) localizes the position of an object in space (D). Fusion of the two retinal images and visual interpretation are association-cortex functions, the accommodation reflex is not initiated by area 17, and an area 17 lesion causes hemianopia rather than agnosia.
questions.keyConcept: Primary visual cortex (area 17) localizes the position of an object in space.
options: Perception of color is the function of visual association cortex.
Visual association cortex is responsible for fusion of the images of both retinas to prevent diplopia.
Primary visual cortex is responsible for initiation of accommodation reflex.
Primary visual cortex localizes the position of object in space.
Lesion in visual cortex area 17 leads to visual agnosia

questions.text: Lesion localized to the left peripheral part of optic chiasma results in:
questions.explanation: The peripheral parts of the optic chiasma carry uncrossed fibers from the temporal retina, which sees the nasal field, so a left peripheral chiasmal lesion causes left nasal hemianopia (A). Central chiasmal lesions cause bitemporal hemianopia.
questions.keyConcept: Left peripheral chiasmal lesion gives left nasal hemianopia.

questions.text: Lesion in anterior part of right optic tract leads to:
questions.explanation: A right optic tract lesion causes left homonymous hemianopia, and because the anterior tract still carries the pupillary light-reflex fibers it gives a hemianopic pupil (B). Macular sparing is a feature of occipital cortical lesions, not tract lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Right optic tract lesion: left homonymous hemianopia with a hemianopic pupil.
options: Left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
Left homonymous hemianopia with hemianopic pupil.
Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
Right homonymous hemianopia with hemianopic pupil.

questions.text: Lesion in the left temporal optic radiations leads to:
questions.explanation: The temporal optic radiations (Meyer loop) carry fibers from the inferior retina, representing the superior visual field, so a left temporal radiation lesion causes a right homonymous superior quadrantanopia (A).
questions.keyConcept: Left temporal optic radiation lesion: right superior homonymous quadrantanopia.
options: Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

questions.text: Which of the following lesions produce right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing:
questions.explanation: A right homonymous hemianopia results from a left retrochiasmal lesion, and macular sparing localizes it specifically to the left primary visual cortex (area 17), owing to its dual blood supply (D).
questions.keyConcept: Right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing: left primary visual cortex.

questions.text: In which of the following lesions no response to light occurs when light comes from the temporal field of the right eye:
questions.explanation: Light from the temporal field of the right eye falls on the right nasal retina, whose fibers cross and run in the left optic tract; a left anterior optic tract lesion, which still carries pupillary fibers, abolishes the light reflex from this field (E). Cortical and radiation lesions spare the reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Light from the right temporal field travels in the left tract; left anterior-tract lesion abolishes its reflex.
options: Left posterior part of optic tract lesion.
Left anterior part of optic tract lesion.

questions.text: Which of the following lesions does NOT produce homonymous hemianopia:
questions.explanation: A chiasmal lesion produces heteronymous (bitemporal) hemianopia, not homonymous, so A is the answer. Lesions of the tract, lateral geniculate body, radiations, and primary cortex all cause homonymous hemianopia.
questions.keyConcept: A chiasmal lesion gives heteronymous (not homonymous) hemianopia.

questions.text: Lesion in the superior part of right area 17 produces:
questions.explanation: The superior bank of area 17 represents the inferior visual field of the contralateral side, so a lesion of the superior part of right area 17 causes a left inferior homonymous quadrantanopia with macular sparing (D).
questions.keyConcept: Superior right area 17 lesion: left inferior homonymous quadrantanopia with macular sparing.
options: Right superior homonymous quadrantanopia with macular sparing.
Left superior homonymous quadrantanopia with macular sparing.
Right inferior homonymous quadrantanopia with macular sparing.
Left inferior homonymous quadrantanopia with macular sparing.

questions.text: Sparing of macular vision occurs with lesion in:
questions.explanation: Macular sparing occurs with lesions of visual area 17 because the macular representation has a dual blood supply (middle and posterior cerebral arteries) (D).
questions.keyConcept: Macular sparing occurs with area 17 (occipital cortex) lesions.

questions.text: Lesion in the occipital areas 18, 19 produces:
questions.explanation: Lesions of the visual association areas 18 and 19 cause visual agnosia -- the person sees but cannot recognize or understand what is seen (E). Blindness and field defects follow area 17 lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Areas 18-19 lesion: visual agnosia (perception without understanding).

questions.text: Regarding color vision:
questions.explanation: Normal trichromats have three cone pigments corresponding to red, green, and blue (B). Color vision is a cone (not rod) function interpreted by the cortex, and color blindness is far commoner in males.
questions.keyConcept: Normal trichromats have three cone pigments (red, green, blue).
options: Normal individuals have pigments corresponding to 3 colors.
Color blindness is common in females than males.
Is the function of the visual association cortex.

questions.text: All of the following play a major role in color vision perception and coding EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Color coding involves cones, small slowly-conducting parvocellular ganglion cells, parvocellular LGB neurons, and cortical blob columns; the rod-dominated peripheral retina plays little role, so E is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: The peripheral (rod) retina plays little role in color coding.
options: Parvocellular neurons in lateral geniculate body.

questions.text: A person who can see deep red color, but sees pale red color as green is:
questions.explanation: Protanomaly is anomalous trichromacy with weak red cones: deep red is still seen, but desaturated pale reds are confused with green (A). Protanopia is the complete absence of red cones.
questions.keyConcept: Protanomaly: deep red seen but pale red confused with green (weak red cones).

questions.text: A person who matches spectral colors by two types of cones only is:
questions.explanation: A dichromat matches all spectral colors using only two cone types because one cone pigment is missing (e.g. protanopia, deuteranopia, tritanopia) (B). Monochromats use one type and anomalous trichromats have three but one is abnormal.
questions.keyConcept: A dichromat matches spectral colors with only two cone types.

questions.text: Binocular vision:
questions.explanation: Binocular vision is the mental fusion into one image of the two slightly different images seen by both eyes at the same time (E). Its sensory requirement is identical images on corresponding points and its motor requirement is balanced extraocular muscles -- the wording in A and B swaps these.
questions.keyConcept: Binocular vision: a single mental image fused from both eyes simultaneously.
options: Its sensory requirements include intact extraocular muscles.
Its motor requirements include intact visual pathway.
It is integrated in the visual association cortex.
It is the function of superior colliculus.
Is the mental impression of 1 image seen by both eyes at the same time.

questions.text: In binocular vision, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Binocular vision is not complete at 6 weeks; it develops gradually and is complete by about 6 years, so C is the exception. It masks a one-eye defect, improves stereoscopic depth, and needs identical images on corresponding points perceived simultaneously.
questions.keyConcept: Binocular vision is not complete at 6 weeks; it matures by about 6 years.
options: It masks the defect in one eye.
It is completely developed at the age of 6 weeks after birth.
In order to occur, images of both eyes must be identical and perceived at the same time by the visual cortex.
It occurs when image of object falls on 2 corresponding retinal points.

questions.text: Critical fusion frequency is:
questions.explanation: Above the critical fusion frequency, successive flashes fuse into a continuous image, the basis of motion pictures and television (E). It is about 50-60 per second, increases with light intensity, and represents fusion (not separate sensation) of stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Above the critical fusion frequency flashes fuse -- the basis of motion pictures.
options: A sensation of separate successive visual stimuli.
Perceived when a continuous source of light is interrupted.
Is the basis of motion pictures.

questions.text: Amblyopia exanopsia is the:
questions.explanation: Amblyopia ex anopsia is the functional cortical suppression of the image from a deviating (squinting) eye to avoid diplopia, and it can become permanent if untreated in childhood (B).
questions.keyConcept: Amblyopia ex anopsia: cortical suppression of a squinting eye's image.
options: Functional cortical suppression of image received from a squinted eye.
Irregularity in curvature of lens and/or cornea.
Mental impression of one image seen clearly by the two eyes.

questions.text: Involuntary visual fixation movement is the function of:
questions.explanation: Involuntary (reflex) visual fixation is a function of the occipital area 19, whereas voluntary fixation and scanning are controlled by the frontal area 8 (E).
questions.keyConcept: Involuntary visual fixation is a function of cortical area 19.

questions.text: Which of the following is a saccadic eye movement:
questions.explanation: Saccades are sudden, rapid, jerky conjugate movements that shift gaze between fixation points (D). Fixation during head rotation is vestibulo-ocular, detailed focusing is fixation/pursuit, convergence is a vergence movement, and optokinetic nystagmus is a separate reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Saccades are sudden rapid jerky conjugate gaze shifts.
options: Focusing on objects to see details

questions.text: Errors of refraction in children can cause eye weakness if not corrected before the age of:
questions.explanation: Uncorrected refractive errors in children can cause amblyopia (lazy eye) if not corrected before about 6 years, the end of the critical period for visual development (C).
questions.keyConcept: Childhood refractive errors cause amblyopia if not corrected before about age 6.

questions.text: The temporal part of optic radiations carry impulses from
questions.explanation: The temporal optic radiations (Meyer loop) carry fibers from the inferior retina, which represents the superior visual field (C).
questions.keyConcept: Temporal optic radiations carry inferior-retina (superior-field) fibers.

questions.text: The macular area of each eye is NOT characterized by being:
questions.explanation: The macula is represented in the primary visual cortex (area 17) posteriorly, not mainly in the association area, so E is the exception. Its representation is separate, large, doubly blood-supplied, and posterior.
questions.keyConcept: The macula is represented in area 17, not mainly the association area.
options: Its area of representation is large.
Its area of representation has double blood supply.
Its area of representation is present posteriorly in area 17.
Is represented mainly in visual association area.

questions.text: Hemianopic scotoma occurs in case of lesion in:
questions.explanation: A unilateral lesion of the posterior (macular) part of area 17 produces a hemianopic scotoma -- a half-field central defect (B). Bilateral posterior lesions give a central scotoma.
questions.keyConcept: Hemianopic scotoma: unilateral lesion of the posterior part of area 17.
options: Bilateral lesion in posterior part of area 17.
Unilateral lesion in posterior part of area 17
Bilateral lesion in posterior part of area 19.
Unilateral lesion in posterior part of area 19.

questions.text: Green cones respond maximally to wave length of:
questions.explanation: Green cones respond maximally near 535 nm (blue around 445-450 nm and red around 570 nm) (D).
questions.keyConcept: Green cones respond maximally near 535 nm.

questions.text: According to Helmohotz theory, color interpretation is the function of:
