questions.explanation: In the Young-Helmholtz trichromatic theory the three cone types are stimulated in different proportions, and the visual cortex interprets these ratios as color (E).
questions.keyConcept: Helmholtz theory: color is interpreted by the visual cortex.
options: Parvocellular neuron in lateral geniculate body.

questions.text: Complete binocular vision development occurs by the age of:
questions.explanation: Binocular vision is completely developed by about 6 years of age (C).
questions.keyConcept: Binocular vision is completely developed by about 6 years.

questions.text: Central scotoma occurs in case of lesion in:
questions.explanation: A central scotoma results from bilateral lesions of the posterior (macular) part of area 17, removing the central macular representation of both sides (A).
questions.keyConcept: Central scotoma: bilateral lesion of the posterior part of area 17.
options: Bilateral lesion in posterior part of area 17.
Unilateral lesion in posterior part of area 17
Bilateral lesion in posterior part of area 19.
Unilateral lesion in posterior part of area 19.

questions.text: Inner part of external auditory canal differs from its outer part in:
questions.explanation: The inner bony part of the external auditory canal lacks ceruminous (wax) glands and hair, unlike the outer cartilaginous part, so E is correct. The outer part is cartilaginous with hair and modified sweat (ceruminous) glands.
questions.keyConcept: Inner (bony) ear canal lacks ceruminous glands and hair, unlike the outer part.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a character of tympanic membrane:
questions.explanation: The tympanic membrane is a resonator that is aperiodic and damped; amplification of sound is achieved by the ossicular lever and area ratio, not by the membrane, so B is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: Amplification is by the ossicles, not the tympanic membrane itself.

questions.text: Aperiodic property of tympanic membrane means that:
questions.explanation: Being aperiodic means the tympanic membrane has no intrinsic natural vibration of its own, so it faithfully reproduces any incoming sound without adding its own frequency (E). Stopping immediately when sound ends is the damped property.
questions.keyConcept: Aperiodic means the tympanic membrane has no intrinsic basal vibration of its own.
options: It is protected from damage by high external temperature.
It vibrates easily and properly in response to sound waves.
Its vibration amplitudes varies according to the intensity of incoming sound waves.
It stops vibration immediately when external sound ends.
It does not have intrinsic basal vibrations.

questions.text: In the middle ear:
questions.explanation: Middle-ear air, replenished via the Eustachian tube, equalizes pressure across the tympanic membrane so it can vibrate freely (D). Air does not limit ossicle movement, the organ of Corti and endolymph are in the inner ear, and the Eustachian tube opens (not closes) on swallowing.
questions.keyConcept: Middle-ear air equalizes pressure across the tympanic membrane.
options: Air limits the movement of boney ossicles.
Organ of corti overlies the vestibular membrane.
Air equalizes the pressure on both sides of drum membrane.
Eustachian tube is closed during swallowing.

questions.text: The boney ossicles:
questions.explanation: The ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) form the ossicular route that conducts sound from the tympanic membrane to the oval window (A). They articulate by synovial joints, increase (not decrease) transmission, the stapes (not malleus) contacts the oval window, and they do not act on the Eustachian tube.
questions.keyConcept: Ossicles form the ossicular route conducting sound to the oval window.
options: Represent the aussicular route for sound transmission.
Their resistance results in decrease intensity of transmission of sound waves.
The malleus is attached to oval window by synovial joints.
Act as a lever system to close the Eustachian tube.

questions.text: Boney ossicles of middle ear do Not play a role in:
questions.explanation: Normal tympanic membrane movement is enabled by pressure equalization via the Eustachian tube, not by the ossicles, so D is the exception. The ossicles provide ossicular transmission, surface-area matching, lever magnification, and impedance matching.
questions.keyConcept: Tympanic membrane movement depends on the Eustachian tube, not the ossicles.
options: Transmission of sound from a high surface area to a low surface area.
Magnification of sound through their lever-like action.
Facilitate normal movement of tympanic membrane.

questions.text: Attenuation acoustic reflex:
questions.explanation: The acoustic (attenuation) reflex has a latency of 40-160 ms, so it cannot protect against sudden short-duration loud sounds such as gunshots (C). It responds to sustained loud sound, dampens (not enhances) vibration, and its efferents run in the facial and trigeminal (not cochlear) nerves.
questions.keyConcept: Acoustic reflex latency means it cannot protect against brief loud sounds.
options: Occurs in response to sound intensity of 100 dB.
It can not protect against high intensity sounds of short duration.
During which, tympanic membrane and oval window vibrations are enhanced.
Efferent impulses to muscles involved in this reflex are carried by facial and cochlear nerves

questions.text: The Eustachian tube:
questions.explanation: The Eustachian tube opens automatically during swallowing, yawning, and ascent in an airplane to equalize pressure (D). It connects the nasopharynx to the middle (not inner) ear, equalizes pressure across the tympanic membrane, and when closed in a cold the drum is retracted inward.
questions.keyConcept: The Eustachian tube opens on swallowing and on ascent in an airplane.
options: Equalizes pressure on sides of oval window.
When closed, as in common cold, the tympanic membrane is pushed outwards.
Opens automatically during swallowing and ascent in an airplane.
Closes automatically when middle ear pressure exceeds atmospheric pressure by 15 mmHg or more.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a middle ear component:
questions.explanation: Ceruminous (wax) glands are in the external auditory canal, not the middle ear, so A is the exception. The middle ear contains air, the stapedius and tensor tympani muscles, the three ossicles, and the opening of the Eustachian tube.
questions.keyConcept: Ceruminous glands are in the ear canal, not the middle ear.

questions.text: Surface area of oval window is smaller than that of tympanic membrane by:
questions.explanation: The effective tympanic membrane area is about 15-17 times larger than the oval window; focusing force onto this smaller area raises pressure for impedance matching, so the oval window is about 15 times smaller (C).
questions.keyConcept: The tympanic membrane area is about 15x larger than the oval window.

questions.text: The acoustic reflex occurs partially during:
questions.explanation: The acoustic reflex is partially activated during vocalization and singing to protect the ear from one's own voice (A).
questions.keyConcept: The acoustic reflex is partially active during vocalization/singing.

questions.text: Normal transmission of sound waves occurs by which sequence:
questions.explanation: Sound passes from the tympanic membrane to the ossicles (malleus-incus-stapes) to the oval window, then into the cochlear fluids (B).
questions.keyConcept: Sound path: tympanic membrane to ossicles to oval window.
options: Tympanic membrane, boney ossicles, round window.
Tympanic membrane, boney ossicles, oval window
Tympanic membrane, oval window, boney ossicles, round window.
Tympanic membrane, boney ossicles, Eustachian tube.
Tympanic membrane, Eustachian tube, oval window.

questions.text: The part of the visual field that has less limitation boundaries is:
questions.explanation: The visual field is least restricted on the temporal side, because the nasal retina extends far and there is no lateral bony obstruction (A); the nasal and superior fields are limited by the nose and brow.
questions.keyConcept: The temporal field is the least restricted part of the visual field.

questions.text: Macular vision is preserved in case of lesion in:
questions.explanation: Macular (central) vision is preserved (macular sparing) with lesions of the primary visual cortex due to its dual blood supply (E).
questions.keyConcept: Macular vision is spared with primary visual cortex lesions.

questions.text: Heteronymous hemianopia occurs in cases of lesion in:
questions.explanation: A lesion of the optic chiasma produces heteronymous (classically bitemporal) hemianopia by interrupting the crossing nasal-retinal fibers (B).
questions.keyConcept: Heteronymous (bitemporal) hemianopia follows an optic chiasma lesion.

questions.text: According to Helmohotz theory, color perception depends on:
questions.explanation: In the Young-Helmholtz theory, color perception depends on the relative frequency of impulses discharged from the three cone types, which the cortex interprets as color (B).
questions.keyConcept: Helmholtz: color depends on impulse frequency from the three cone types.
options: Frequency of impulses discharged from different types of cones.
Parvocellular neurons in lateral geniculate body.

questions.text: Object in the visual field of one eye only is considered an area of:
questions.explanation: A region seen by one eye only (the temporal crescents) is the area of monocular vision; the overlap seen by both eyes is binocular (C).
questions.keyConcept: A region seen by one eye only is monocular vision.

questions.text: These structures help in proper conduction of sound waves, EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The external canal, tympanic membrane, ossicles (incus), and Eustachian tube help conduct sound; the organ of Corti is the inner-ear sensory transducer, not a conducting structure, so D is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: The organ of Corti transduces sound; it does not conduct it.

questions.text: Middle ear muscles help in:
questions.explanation: The middle-ear muscles (stapedius, tensor tympani) contract reflexly to attenuate transmission of loud, high-intensity sound, protecting the inner ear (E).
questions.keyConcept: Middle-ear muscles attenuate transmission of loud sounds.
options: Conduction of sound waves to the inner ear.
Equalization of pressure across the tympanic membrane.
Magnification of sound transmission to match the inner ear high impedance.
Production of proper displacement of oval window.
Attenuation of high intensity sound transmission.

questions.text: Eustachian tube is NOT characterized by:
questions.explanation: The Eustachian tube does not amplify sound, so D is the exception. It is about 3.5 cm long, equalizes pressure across the tympanic membrane, drains middle-ear secretions, and opens on swallowing.
questions.keyConcept: The Eustachian tube does not amplify sound (that is the ossicles' role).
options: Equalize the pressure across the tympanic membrane.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT involved in the tympanic reflex:
questions.explanation: The tympanic (attenuation acoustic) reflex involves the tensor tympani, the olivocochlear/facial pathways, and hair-cell input; the round window is a passive pressure-relief membrane and is not part of the reflex, so B is the answer.
questions.keyConcept: The round window is not part of the tympanic (acoustic) reflex.

questions.text: During transmission of sound waves:
questions.explanation: The lever action of the ossicles contributes about 1.3-fold magnification while the tympanic-to-oval-window area ratio contributes about 17-fold, giving roughly 22-fold total (C). The oval window is smaller (not larger) than the tympanic membrane, and the middle-ear muscles attenuate transmission.
questions.keyConcept: Ossicular lever adds about 1.3x; the area ratio adds about 17x.
options: Boney ossicles amplify sounds by total magnification of 17 times.
Surface area of oval window is larger than that of tympanic membrane by 20-22 times.
Lever action of boney ossicles is responsible for transmission of sound with 1.3 magnification.
Middle ear muscles contract reflex to help sound transmission.
Tympanic membrane vibration continue for a time after stoppage of external sound.

questions.text: Which of these is NOT a component of inner ear:
questions.explanation: The malleus is a middle-ear ossicle, not part of the inner ear, so E is the exception. The modiolus, basilar membrane, organ of Corti, and endolymphatic duct are inner-ear structures.
questions.keyConcept: The malleus is a middle-ear ossicle, not an inner-ear component.

questions.text: The bony axis of the cochlea contains:
questions.explanation: The modiolus, the bony central axis of the cochlea, houses the spiral ganglion (cell bodies of the cochlear nerve) (D). Perilymph, endolymph, the organ of Corti, and hair cells lie within the cochlear canals.
questions.keyConcept: The modiolus houses the spiral ganglion of the cochlear nerve.

questions.text: Communication between scala vestibule and scala tympani occurs through:
questions.explanation: The scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate at the apex of the cochlea through the helicotrema (A).
questions.keyConcept: Scala vestibuli and scala tympani communicate at the apex via the helicotrema.

questions.text: The receptor of hearing is located in:
questions.explanation: The organ of Corti, the receptor of hearing, rests on the basilar membrane (B).
questions.keyConcept: The organ of Corti (hearing receptor) rests on the basilar membrane.

questions.text: The cochlear duct is:
questions.explanation: The cochlear duct (scala media) is bounded by the vestibular (Reissner) membrane above and the basilar membrane below (B). It is filled with endolymph, lies in the middle, is not closed by the foramen ovale, and is auditory (not vestibular).
questions.keyConcept: The cochlear duct lies between the vestibular and basilar membranes.
options: Vestibular and basilar membranes form its sides.
Present in the lower part of cochlea.
A part of the vestibular apparatus.

questions.text: Inner hair cells are NOT characterized by being:
questions.explanation: Electromotility, the active mechanical feedback on the basilar membrane, is a property of OUTER hair cells, so E is the exception for inner cells. Inner hair cells number about 3500, are in one row, receive most afferent fibers, and perform sound transduction.
questions.keyConcept: Electromotility is an outer-hair-cell property, not an inner-hair-cell one.
options: Innervated by majority of cochlear nerve afferent fibers.
Their electro-motility affects vibration of basilar membrane.

questions.text: Outer hair cells are characterized by being:
questions.explanation: Outer hair cells show electromotility, lengthening and shortening to amplify and tune basilar-membrane vibration (the cochlear amplifier) (E). The ~3500 count, single row, most afferents, and transduction describe inner hair cells.
questions.keyConcept: Outer hair cells show electromotility that amplifies basilar-membrane motion.
options: Innervated by majority of cochlear nerve afferent fibers.
Their electro-motility produces mechanical effect on vibrations of basilar membrane.

questions.text: Regarding sound:
questions.explanation: Sound intensity in decibels is expressed relative to a standard reference sound (D). Amplitude determines loudness (not pitch), 0 dB is the threshold (not absence) of sound, the human range is about 20-20,000 Hz, and frequency is measured in Hz.
questions.keyConcept: Sound intensity (dB) is expressed relative to a standard reference sound.
options: Zero dB means absence of sound.
Human can hear frequencies of 20 – 200.000 Hz.
Sound intensity is calculated with reference to a standard sound.
Frequency of sound is measured by dB.

questions.text: In the auditory portion of the inner ear:
questions.explanation: The olivocochlear bundle supplies efferent fibers (mainly to outer hair cells) that modulate cochlear sensitivity and hearing quality (E). Scala media has high K+ (not Na+), hair-cell bases sit in low-K+ fluid, the scala tympani is closed by the round (not oval) window, and inner (not outer) hair cells transduce.
questions.keyConcept: The olivocochlear bundle gives efferents that modulate hearing.
options: High sodium concentration is found in the scala media.
Bases of hair cells of organ of Corti are bathed by high potassium fluid.
Scala tympani is closed by oval window.
Outer hair cells transduce sound vibrations into action potential.
Olivocochlear bundle gives efferent innervation to modulate hearing quality.

questions.text: Regarding hearing:
questions.explanation: A greater basilar-membrane displacement (louder sound) increases the frequency of impulses in the cochlear nerve, encoding intensity (C). High frequencies stimulate the base (not apex), the receptor potential is depolarizing, outer hair cells amplify, and inner hair cells are fewer than outer.
questions.keyConcept: Greater basilar-membrane displacement raises cochlear-nerve impulse frequency.
options: High frequency sound stimulates cochlea near its apex.
Receptor potential of hearing receptors is hyperpolarization.
The greater the displacement of basilar membrane, the greater frequency of impulses generated in cochlear nerve.
Outer hair cells primary function is to respond to displacement of basilar membrane by generating impulses.
Inner hair cells are more numerous than outer hair cells.

questions.text: The cochlear duct fluid potential difference in respect to cochlear hair cells is:
questions.explanation: The endolymph is about +80 mV and the hair-cell interior about -70 mV, giving a potential difference of roughly +150 mV across the apical membrane, the driving force for transduction (E).
questions.keyConcept: Endolymph (+80) and hair cell (-70) give about +150 mV across the apex.

questions.text: Cochlear microphonic potential is the:
questions.explanation: The cochlear microphonic is the depolarizing receptor potential generated by the hair cells, which follows the waveform of the sound (B).
questions.keyConcept: Cochlear microphonic = the depolarizing receptor potential of hair cells.
options: Depolarizing receptor potential of hair cells.
Hyperpolarizing receptor potential of hair cells.
Depolarizing potential changes in cochlear nerve fibers around bases of hair cells.
Hyperpolarizing potential changes in cochlear nerve fibers around bases of hair cells.

questions.text: Regarding hearing:
questions.explanation: Efferent fibers (the olivocochlear bundle and the reflex supply to middle-ear muscles) arise within the auditory pathway and modulate inner- and middle-ear function (A). Infranuclear lesions cause marked deafness, area 22 handles interpretation, the cortex alone cannot pinpoint a source, and area 41 (not 22) is the primary auditory area.
questions.keyConcept: Auditory efferents arise in the pathway to modulate middle and inner ears.
options: Efferents arise from an area in the auditory pathway to affect functions of middle and inner ears.
Infranuclear lesion results in slight hearing impairments.
Lesion in area 22 causes inability to discriminate sound intensity and pitch.
Auditory association area can localize the exact source of sound.
Auditory area 41 lesion produces auditory aphasia.

questions.text: Regarding hearing:
questions.explanation: Depolarization of hair cells opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and Ca2+ influx triggers glutamate release onto the cochlear nerve (E). The basilar membrane is more elastic than the tectorial, deflection toward the tallest stereocilium depolarizes, shearing acts on the tectorial membrane, and cation entry causes the depolarization.
questions.keyConcept: Hair-cell depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca++ channels, releasing glutamate.
options: The basilar membrane is less elastic than the tectorial membrane.
Deflection of steriocilia away from the taller steriocilium produces depolarization of hair cells.
Shearing forces of cilia on the under surface of vestibular membrane produces opening of cation channels.
Opening of mechanically gated cation channels in hair cells lead to release of glutamate.
Depolarization of hair cells results in opening of voltage-gated Ca++ channels and Ca++ influx.

questions.text: The electromotility of outer hair cells lead to:
questions.explanation: Outer-hair-cell electromotility sharpens frequency tuning and suppresses background noise to clarify a specific sound (the cochlear amplifier) (D). The cells shorten when depolarized and elongate when hyperpolarized, but their role is amplification and tuning, not generating the nerve impulse or simple protection.
questions.keyConcept: Outer-hair-cell electromotility suppresses background noise to clarify sound.
options: Their depolarization and generation of a nerve impulse in cochlear nerve.
Their elongation when hyperpolarized to improve vibrations of basilar membrane.
Their shortening when depolarized to decrease vibrations of basilar membrane.
Block of background noises to clarify a specific sound.

questions.text: Regarding Sound discrimination:
questions.explanation: Sound localization depends on the interaural differences in time of arrival and intensity of the signals reaching the auditory cortex (A). Intensity is coded by impulse frequency (not AP amplitude), frequency discrimination uses place plus traveling-wave mechanisms, and is not purely cortical.
questions.keyConcept: Sound localization uses interaural time and intensity differences.
options: Discrimination of locality depends on the intensity and time of arrival of impulses reaching the auditory cortex.
Discrimination of intensity depends on the amplitude of action potential generated in VIIIth cranial nerve.
Intensity discrimination depends on the travelling wave and the place theories.
Frequency discrimination is entirely a function of the auditory cortex.
Low frequency sound stimulates outer hair cells more than inner hair cells.

questions.text: Regarding hearing:
questions.explanation: The superior olivary nucleus gives rise to the olivocochlear efferents to the inner ear and connects to the motor nuclei of the middle-ear muscles (C). Each cochlea is represented bilaterally in the temporal (not parietal) lobe, the spiral ganglion is the 1st-order neuron, the medial (not lateral) geniculate is the auditory relay, and area 41 is primary.
questions.keyConcept: The superior olivary nucleus gives efferents to inner ear and middle-ear muscles.
options: Each cochlea is bilaterally represented in the parietal lobe.
The cochlear nuclei represent the 1st order neuron in the auditory pathway.
Superior olivary nucleus sends efferent to inner ear and to nerves supplying middle ear muscles.
Lateral geniculate body is the 3rd order neuron in the auditory pathway.
Cortical area 22 is the 1ry area responsible for auditory discrimination.

questions.text: The following causes result in conductive deafness EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Meniere disease (endolymphatic hydrops) causes sensorineural deafness, not conductive, so B is the exception. Otitis externa/wax, otosclerosis, nasopharyngeal tumor, and adenoids cause conductive deafness.
questions.keyConcept: Meniere disease causes sensorineural (not conductive) deafness.

questions.text: The following causes result in sensori-neural deafness EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Exostosis (bony canal overgrowth) obstructs the external canal and causes conductive deafness, so C is the exception. Congenital and natal infections, vascular insufficiency, brain tumor or head injury, and raised endolymph pressure cause sensorineural deafness.
questions.keyConcept: Exostosis causes conductive (not sensorineural) deafness.
options: Congenital, natal and postnatal infections such as measles.

questions.text: Which of the following is a hearing quantitative test:
questions.explanation: Audiometry gives a quantitative measurement of hearing thresholds across frequencies (A). The Rinne, Weber, watch, and whisper tests are qualitative.
questions.keyConcept: Audiometry is the quantitative hearing test.

questions.text: Age-related decrease hearing acuity is:
questions.explanation: Age-related hearing loss (presbycusis) is due largely to reduced elasticity of the basilar membrane and loss of hair cells (B). It is presbycusis (not presbyopia) and is not due to more outer hair cells.
questions.keyConcept: Presbycusis is due to reduced basilar-membrane elasticity (and hair-cell loss).
options: Due to decrease elasticity of basilar membrane.
Due to increase number of outer hair cells relative to the number of inner hair cells.
Due to damage of spiral ganglion.
Due to degeneration in auditory cortical areas.

questions.text: Locality discrimination by the auditory cortex depends on:
questions.explanation: The auditory cortex localizes sound from the interaural differences in time of arrival and loudness between the two ears (D).
questions.keyConcept: Locality discrimination uses interaural time and loudness differences.
options: The place where the basilar membrane is maximally displaced.
The frequency of impulses discharged in the cochlear nerve.
The difference in time and in loudness of sound between the two ears.

questions.text: Discrimination of pitch of a sound is:
questions.explanation: Pitch (frequency) discrimination depends mainly on which part of the basilar membrane is maximally displaced (the place principle): the base for high and the apex for low frequencies (B).
questions.keyConcept: Pitch discrimination depends on the maximally displaced part of the basilar membrane.
options: Related to the part of the basilar membrane that displaced maximally.
Depends on the frequency of impulses reaching the auditory cortex.
Depends on the fact that sound arrives earlier and louder to the closer ear.
Is the function of the basilar membrane of the cochlea.

questions.text: Regarding taste sensation:
questions.explanation: Taste receptor cells are modified epithelial cells that are continuously renewed (about every 10 days) (E). Sweet is at the tip, bitter at the back, sour is from H+, and salty is from Na+, so the other pairings are wrong.
questions.keyConcept: Taste receptors are rapidly renewed modified epithelial cells.
options: Sweet receptors are on the edges of tongue.
Bitter receptors are on the tip of tongue.
Salty receptors are stimulated by H+ in solution.
Sour receptors are located on the dorsum of the tongue.
Taste receptors are rapidly regenerated modified epithelial cells.

questions.text: Which mechanism is Not true in stimulation of taste receptors:
questions.explanation: Sweet receptors are metabotropic (G-protein-coupled), not ionotropic Na+ channels, so A is the false statement. Salt depolarizes via Na+ leak channels, sour via H+ closing K+ channels, bitter via metabotropic Ca2+ rise, and umami via metabotropic glutamate receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Sweet receptors are metabotropic, not ionotropic Na+ channels.
options: Sweet receptors are ionotropic that directly allow Na+ influx.
Ionized salts depolarize their receptors directly through leakage channels.
H+ in solution depolarize its receptors through closure of K+ channels.
Bitter stimulating substances bind to metabotropic receptor to increase intracellular Ca++.
Umami taste is a result of stimulation of metabotropic glutamate receptor.

questions.text: Which type of cells is responsible for renewal of taste cells:
questions.explanation: Basal cells of the taste bud divide to renew the taste receptor (gustatory) cells (A).
questions.keyConcept: Basal cells renew the taste receptor cells.

questions.text: Sweet receptors are stimulated by:
questions.explanation: Sweet receptors are stimulated by sugars and also by alcohols and aldehydes (and some amino acids and ketones) (E). Cations relate to salt, H+ to sour, and alkaloids and caffeine to bitter.
questions.keyConcept: Sweet receptors are stimulated by sugars, alcohols, and aldehydes.

questions.text: Salt receptors are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Salt receptors depolarize directly when Na+ enters through leak (ENaC) channels (C). They are at the tip and sides, are ionotropic (not metabotropic or cAMP-driven), and are stimulated by Na+ (not H+).
questions.keyConcept: Salt receptors depolarize directly via Na+ leak channels.
options: Located at the tip of tongue.
Depolarize directly by Na+ influx through leaky channels.
Activated through increase in c.AMP concentration.

questions.text: Umami receptors are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Umami (glutamate) acts on a metabotropic receptor that raises intracellular IP3 and Ca2+ (E). It is broadly distributed, not stimulated by salts, not a direct Na+ channel, and not cAMP-mediated.
questions.keyConcept: Umami acts via a metabotropic receptor raising IP3 and Ca++.
options: Present at the back of tongue.
Activated by an increase in their c.AMP concentration.
Their stimulation leads to intracellular increase in inositol triphosphate and Ca++ levels.

questions.text: Regarding olfaction:
questions.explanation: Olfactory receptors are true bipolar nerve cells (neurons) in the olfactory epithelium (B). They are rapidly (not slowly) adapting, confined to the roof of the nasal cavity, depolarize (not hyperpolarize) on stimulation, and conduct Na+ and Ca2+ inward.
questions.keyConcept: Olfactory receptors are true bipolar nerve cells.
options: Olfactory receptors are widely distributed in the whole nasal cavity.
Olfactory receptors response to stimulation is hyperpolarization.
Chloride influx occurs in olfactory receptors when stimulated.

questions.text: The mechanism that brings olfactory receptors to threshold depolarization is:
questions.explanation: After cAMP opens cation channels, the resulting Ca2+ entry opens Ca2+-activated Cl- channels, and Cl- efflux gives the amplifying depolarization that reaches threshold (D).
questions.keyConcept: Ca++-activated Cl- channels bring olfactory receptors to threshold.
options: Opening of Ca++ dependent Cl- channels.

questions.text: Olfactory receptor renewal occurs every:
questions.explanation: Olfactory receptor neurons are renewed about every 2 months (60 days) from basal stem cells (B), which is unusual for neurons.
questions.keyConcept: Olfactory receptor neurons are renewed about every 2 months.

questions.text: Partial initial depolarization of olfactory receptors occurs through:
questions.explanation: Odorant binding activates a G-protein (Golf) and adenylyl cyclase, raising cAMP, which opens cyclic-nucleotide-gated cation channels to give the initial partial depolarization (B).
questions.keyConcept: Initial olfactory depolarization: cAMP opens cation channels.
options: c.AMP mediated opening of cation channels.
Opening of Ca++ activated Cl- channels.
Opening of voltage gated Ca++ channels.

questions.text: Smell receptor adaptation occurs rapidly through:
questions.explanation: Rapid olfactory adaptation occurs as the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger extrudes Ca2+, closing the Ca2+-activated Cl- channels and ending the response (D).
questions.keyConcept: Olfactory adaptation: the Na+/Ca++ exchanger removes Ca++.

questions.text: Abnormal smell, in absence of stimuli is termed:
questions.explanation: Paraosmia is a perceived abnormal or distorted smell, including smelling odors in the absence of a real stimulus (C). Anosmia is loss of smell, hyposmia is reduced smell, and ageusia/dysgeusia are taste disorders.
questions.keyConcept: Paraosmia = a perceived abnormal smell, even without a real stimulus.

questions.text: Which sentence is true about the inner ear:
questions.explanation: The scala media is filled with endolymph, an unusual intracellular-like, K+-rich fluid (C). The scala vestibuli has perilymph (not endolymph), the scala tympani is not the endocochlear duct, the organ of Corti overlies the basilar (not vestibular) membrane, and the basilar membrane is more elastic than the tectorial.
questions.keyConcept: Scala media holds endolymph -- an intracellular-like, K+-rich fluid.
options: Scala tympani is the endocochlear duct.
Scala media contains an intracellular-like, K+-rich fluid.
Organ of Corti overlies the vestibular membrane.
Basilar membrane is less elastic than tectorial membrane.

questions.text: Inner hair cells are characterized by:
questions.explanation: Inner hair cells are the true auditory transducers, converting basilar-membrane motion into receptor potentials and afferent impulses (E). Most efferents and electromotility belong to outer hair cells, and deflection toward the tallest stereocilium depolarizes.
questions.keyConcept: Inner hair cells are responsible for auditory transduction.
options: Receive majority of efferent from olivo-cochlear bundle.
Stimulated when taller steriocilium bends towards the smaller ones.

questions.text: Regarding characters of sounds:
questions.explanation: The decibel scale is logarithmic: 20 dB represents a 10-fold pressure or 100-fold intensity ratio above the reference (B). The standard sound is a reference intensity (not minimal frequency), humans can hear 120 dB (painfully), amplitude sets loudness (not pitch), and loudness is in dB (not Hz).
questions.keyConcept: 20 dB is a 100-fold intensity ratio above the reference sound.
options: Standard sound is the minimal audible frequency.
A sound of 20 dB is stronger than reference sound by 100 folds.
Human can not hear sounds of 120 dB intensity.
Sound loudness id measured by Hz units.

questions.text: Receptor potential of auditory hair cells is:
questions.explanation: The hair-cell receptor potential arises when stereocilia deflection opens mechanically-gated cation channels, allowing K+ (and some Ca2+) influx and depolarization (D). It is depolarizing (not hyperpolarizing), promotes (not inhibits) glutamate release, and is not the endocochlear potential.
questions.keyConcept: Hair-cell receptor potential: opening of mechanically-gated cation channels.
options: Inhibits release of glutamate from hair cells.
Occurs by opening of mechanically-gated cation channels.

questions.text: Hair cells electromotility:
questions.explanation: Electromotility of outer hair cells actively alters basilar-membrane displacement, amplifying and sharpening the response (E). It is a property of outer (not inner) cells, the cells shorten on depolarization, and it is for amplification and tuning rather than releasing glutamate or simple protection.
questions.keyConcept: Outer-hair-cell electromotility alters basilar-membrane displacement.
options: Is a property of inner hair cells.
Impulses affect hair cells through releasing glutamate.
It is protective against high intensity loud sounds.
It affects the degree of displacement of basilar membrane.

questions.text: Which of the following is Not a part of the auditory pathway:
questions.explanation: The inferior olivary nucleus belongs to the olivocerebellar (motor) system, not the auditory pathway, so C is the exception. The spiral ganglion, cochlear nuclei, inferior colliculus, and medial geniculate body are auditory relays.
questions.keyConcept: The inferior olivary nucleus is not part of the auditory pathway.

questions.text: Regarding stimulation of taste receptors:
questions.explanation: Sweet receptors are metabotropic (G-protein-coupled) receptors (A). Sour is via H+ (not cAMP), bitter via metabotropic Ca2+ (not H+ through Na+ channels), salt via Na+ leak (not IP3), and umami is metabotropic (not an ion channel).
questions.keyConcept: Sweet receptors are metabotropic (G-protein-coupled) receptors.
options: Sour receptors are stimulated by increase intracellular c.AMP.
Bitter receptors are stimulated by influx of H+ through Na+ channels.
Salt receptors stimulation increases intrareceptor IP3.

questions.text: Gustatory receptors are:
questions.explanation: Gustatory receptor cells are renewed about every 10 days (C). They are modified epithelial cells (not bipolar neurons), found on the palate and epiglottis as well as the tongue, depolarize (not hyperpolarize) on stimulation, and respond to dissolved (not volatile) substances.
questions.keyConcept: Gustatory receptor cells are renewed about every 10 days.

questions.text: During olfactory transduction:
questions.explanation: In olfactory transduction, cAMP-gated cation entry raises Ca2+, which opens Ca2+-sensitive Cl- channels; the Cl- efflux amplifies depolarization enough to fire the olfactory nerve (C). Receptors depolarize (not hyperpolarize), by cation influx (not outflux), odorants must be water- and lipid-soluble, and cAMP increases (not decreases).
questions.keyConcept: Olfactory: Ca++-sensitive Cl- channels amplify the receptor potential.
options: Intrareceptor cation outflux depolarize olfactory cells.
Opening of Ca++-sensitive Cl- channels brings the receptor potential to a level adequate to generate impulses in the olfactory nerve.
Decrease intrareceptor cAMP mediate olfactory transduction.

questions.text: Rapid adaptation of olfactory receptors is explained by:
questions.explanation: Rapid olfactory adaptation is due to extrusion of Ca2+ by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, which closes the Ca2+-activated Cl- channels and terminates the response (A).
questions.keyConcept: Rapid olfactory adaptation: the Na+/Ca++ exchanger extrudes Ca++.
options: Removal of Ca++ by Na+-Ca++ exchanger.
Removal of Na+ by Na+-K+ pump.
Removal of K+ by K+ channels.
Removal of Cl- by Cl- exchanger.

questions.text: All the following are true regarding balance, EXCEPT:-
questions.explanation: Deceleration is a change in velocity that disturbs posture and does evoke vestibular reflexes, so E is the false statement. Posture is static balance, equilibrium is dynamic balance, balance reflexes integrate at several CNS levels, and acceleration may be angular or linear.
questions.keyConcept: Deceleration disturbs posture and does evoke vestibular reflexes.
options: Posture is the static balance during rest
Equilibrium is the balance during movement
Reflexes responsible for balance, posture and equilibrium are integrated at different CNS levels
Acceleration may be angular or straight
Deceleration is not associated with reflexes because it is not associated with disturbed posture.

questions.text: Vestibular apparatus:
questions.explanation: The vestibular apparatus detects linear and angular acceleration and deceleration and the effect of gravity (C). It is the non-auditory part of the labyrinth, does not initiate voluntary movement, does participate in acceleration perception, and does not control the proprioceptors.
questions.keyConcept: The vestibular apparatus detects acceleration, deceleration, and gravity.
options: Represent the auditory part of the labyrinth.
Function to initiate the voluntary movements.
Contains receptors concerned with detection of acceleration, deceleration and effects of gravitational forces.
Has no role in perception of acceleration.

questions.text: Vestibular apparatus:
questions.explanation: The vestibular apparatus detects changes in the rate and direction of head position and movement (E). It contains the semicircular canals AND the otolith organs, discharges along the vestibular nerve only, the cochlea is auditory, and it influences mainly axial antigravity muscle tone.
questions.keyConcept: The vestibular apparatus detects the rate and direction of head movement.
options: Contains two types of sensory organs, crista and macula that discharge impulses along the 8th and 10th cranial nerves.
The cochlea is its main component.
Can discharge impulses that affect muscle tone in distal muscles of the limbs.
Detect changes in rate and direction of head position and movements.

questions.text: The receptors of postural reflexes include all of the following except:
questions.explanation: Inner hair cells are auditory (cochlear) receptors and play no postural role, so C is the exception. Muscle spindles, the retina (rods and cones), the crista ampullaris, and the macula all contribute to postural reflexes.
questions.keyConcept: Inner hair cells are auditory, not postural-reflex, receptors.

questions.text: All the following are components of the vestibular apparatus, except :-
questions.explanation: The vestibular nucleus is a brainstem central connection, not a peripheral component of the vestibular apparatus, so C is the exception. The crista ampullaris, vestibular hair cells, macula, and saccule are parts of the apparatus.
questions.keyConcept: The vestibular nucleus is central, not a peripheral component of the apparatus.

questions.text: The semi-circular canals:
questions.explanation: The semicircular canals detect angular (rotational) acceleration (B). There are 3 (not 3 pairs) on each side, they are filled with K+-rich endolymph, their hair cells depolarize with K+ entry on cupula deflection, and they open into the utricle (not saccule).
questions.keyConcept: The semicircular canals detect angular (rotational) acceleration.
options: Filled with fluid rich in Na+ ions.
Its receptors show depolarization when mainly Ca++ influx occurs in the apical border of its hair cells.

questions.text: Vestibular hair cells:-
questions.explanation: Vestibular hair cells are mechanoreceptors sensitive to bending of their stereocilia (D). They have stereocilia plus one kinocilium, are innervated by the vestibular nerve, release transmitter onto the afferents, and not all are stimulated by rotation (the maculae respond to gravity and linear acceleration).
questions.keyConcept: Vestibular hair cells are mechanoreceptors sensitive to bending.
options: Are provided with the same type of cilia all over their surface
Are innervated by cochlear nerve fibers
Are stimulated by a chemical transmitter released from the terminals of the innervating nerve fibers
Are all stimulated by rotational forces.

questions.text: The hair cells in the vestibular receptor organs:
questions.explanation: All vestibular hair cells are mechanosensitive (D). They are not stimulated only during acceleration, deflection toward the kinocilium depolarizes while deflection away hyperpolarizes, and only the maculae (not the cristae) carry calcium-carbonate otoconia.
questions.keyConcept: All vestibular hair cells are mechanosensitive receptors.
options: Show hyper-polarization when sterocillia deviated towards kinocillium.
Show depolarization when sterocillia deviated away from kinocillium.
All have Ca++ carbonate crystals in their gelatinous covering.

questions.text: All of the following statements about the vestibular apparatus are true, EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Control of muscle tone during fine skilled movement is a cerebellar and cortical function, not a vestibular one, so E is the exception. The apparatus comprises the semicircular canals plus the utricle and saccule, the canals contain cristae, and the otolith organs detect linear acceleration and head position relative to gravity.
questions.keyConcept: Fine skilled-movement control is cerebellar, not vestibular.
options: It consists of semicircular canals and two small sacs, utricle and saccule.
The semicircular canals contain sensory organs called crista.
The utricle and saccule are concerned with perception of linear acceleration.
The receptors of utricle and saccule detect head position relative to gravitational forces.
Concerned with regulation of muscle tone during performance of fine skilled movement.

questions.text: The central connections of the vestibular apparatus include all of the following, EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The vestibular central connections include the cerebellum, reticular formation, the medial longitudinal bundles bilaterally, and the superior temporal gyrus; the limbic cortex is not a primary vestibular connection, so D is the exception.
questions.keyConcept: The limbic cortex is not a primary vestibular central connection.
options: Medial longitudinal bundle on both sides.

questions.text: Endolymph:
questions.explanation: Endolymph fills the membranous labyrinth (A). It is K+-rich, electrically positive (not negative) relative to perilymph, its inertia is essential for stimulating the canal receptors during rotation, and it does not differ in density between crista and macula.
questions.keyConcept: Endolymph fills the membranous labyrinth.
options: It is found within the membranous labyrinth.
Has a K+ concentration closes to that of the extra-cellular fluid.
Is electrically negative with respect to the perilymph.
Its inertia has no role in the stimulation of receptors in the semicircular canals during rotation.
In crista ampullaris, it is of high density than in the macula.

questions.text: The hair cells in the semicircular canals are stimulated by:
questions.explanation: Semicircular-canal hair cells are stimulated when endolymph movement (its inertia during angular acceleration) deflects the cupula relative to the hair cells (D). Perilymph movement, linear acceleration, constant velocity, and gravity do not stimulate them.
questions.keyConcept: Canal hair cells respond to endolymph movement relative to them.
options: Movement of the endolymph relative to the hair cells.

questions.text: Which vestibular receptor detects head angular acceleration in the shoulder to shoulder vertical plane:
questions.explanation: Rotation in the shoulder-to-shoulder vertical (roll) plane is detected by the crista of the posterior semicircular canal (B).
questions.keyConcept: The posterior SCC detects roll (shoulder-to-shoulder) rotation.
options: Crista ampullaris of anterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of posterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of horizontal semicircular canals.

questions.text: Which vestibular receptor detects head angular acceleration in the front to back antero-posterior plane:
questions.explanation: Rotation in the front-to-back (pitch) plane is detected by the crista of the anterior (superior) semicircular canal (A).
questions.keyConcept: The anterior SCC detects pitch (front-to-back) rotation.
options: Crista ampullaris of anterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of posterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of horizontal semicircular canals.

questions.text: Which vestibular receptor detects head angular acceleration in the side-to-side plane:
questions.explanation: Rotation in the horizontal side-to-side (yaw) plane is detected by the crista of the horizontal (lateral) semicircular canal (C).
questions.keyConcept: The horizontal SCC detects yaw (side-to-side) rotation.
options: Crista ampullaris of anterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of posterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of horizontal semicircular canals.

questions.text: Which vestibular receptor detects head deviation from the vertical plane:
questions.explanation: The macula of the utricle, horizontally oriented, detects head deviation or tilt from the vertical and detects horizontal linear acceleration (D).
questions.keyConcept: The utricular macula detects deviation from the vertical plane.
options: Crista ampullaris of anterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of posterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of horizontal semicircular canals.

questions.text: Which vestibular receptor detects head deviation from the horizontal plane:
questions.explanation: The macula of the saccule, vertically oriented, detects head deviation from the horizontal plane and detects vertical linear acceleration (E).
questions.keyConcept: The saccular macula detects deviation from the horizontal plane.
options: Crista ampullaris of anterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of posterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of horizontal semicircular canals.

questions.text: Which vestibular receptor detects linear acceleration when you are present in a moving car:
questions.explanation: Horizontal linear acceleration, as in a moving car, is detected by the macula of the utricle (D).
questions.keyConcept: The utricular macula detects horizontal linear acceleration (a moving car).
options: Crista ampullaris of anterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of posterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of horizontal semicircular canals.

questions.text: Which vestibular receptor detects linear acceleration when you are using the elevator:
questions.explanation: Vertical linear acceleration, as in an elevator, is detected by the macula of the saccule (E).
questions.keyConcept: The saccular macula detects vertical linear acceleration (an elevator).
options: Crista ampullaris of anterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of posterior semicircular canals.
Crista ampullaris of horizontal semicircular canals.

questions.text: About the utricles, all of the following are true, EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The utricle can initiate reflex changes in muscle tone (righting reflexes), so D is the false statement. It is stimulated by head position relative to gravity, contains hair cells, has endolymph continuous with the rest of the labyrinth, and detects forward and backward tilt.
questions.keyConcept: The utricle can initiate reflex changes in muscle tone.
options: Are stimulated by head position relative to gravity.
Contain endolymph which communicates with that in the SCCs and cochlea.
Can not initiate reflex changes in muscle tone.
Detect head front and back tilting.

questions.text: The crista ampullaris is sensitive to:-
questions.explanation: The crista ampullaris is sensitive to rotational (angular) acceleration (D), not to sound, gravity, or linear acceleration.
questions.keyConcept: The crista ampullaris is sensitive to rotational acceleration.
options: Movement of the head in space

questions.text: Hair cells of the cristae are stimulated by:-
questions.explanation: Crista hair cells are excited (depolarized) when their stereocilia bend toward the kinocilium (C); bending away hyperpolarizes them.
questions.keyConcept: Crista hair cells are excited by stereocilia bending toward the kinocilium.
options: Bending of their stereocilia toward any direction
Movement of perilymph in any direction
Bending of stereocilia away from kinocilium
Bending of the steriocilia towards the otoconia

questions.text: All of the following regarding the crista ampullaris are true, EXCEPT:-
questions.explanation: Orientation of head position relative to gravity is a function of the maculae (otolith organs), not the crista, so E is the exception. The crista has a cupula of endolymph density, is a mechanoreceptor, has a kinocilium with uniformly arranged stereocilia, and responds to rotational acceleration.
questions.keyConcept: Orientation of head position is a macular (not crista) function.
options: Contains cupula that has the same endolymph density
Contains Kinocilium and uniformly arranged steriocilia
Stimulated by acceleration in a rotatory fashion
It is very important in orientation of the head position in space

questions.text: Asymmetrical discharge between the SCCs of both body sides occurs:-
questions.explanation: Asymmetry in discharge between the two sides' canals occurs at the start, on a change of speed, and at the end of rotation (during angular acceleration and deceleration) (D); at constant speed and in linear motion the discharge is symmetrical.
questions.keyConcept: SCC discharge is asymmetrical at start, speed change, and end of rotation.
options: In the start, change in speed and end of rotational acceleration

questions.text: Vertigo:-
questions.explanation: After rotation stops, endolymph momentum deflects the cupula oppositely, producing a false sensation of rotation toward the opposite side -- post-rotational vertigo (A).
questions.keyConcept: Vertigo: a post-rotational false sense of turning the opposite way.
options: Is a post-rotational sense of being rotated toward opposite side of original rotation
Is a post-rotational sense of being rotated toward same side of original rotation
Is a pre-rotational sense of being rotated toward opposite side of original rotation
Is a pre-rotational sense of being rotated toward same side of original rotation
It is a rotational sense that is lost after 30 sec of constant speed rotation

questions.text: All of the following is true regarding Vertigo, EXCEPT:-
questions.explanation: Vertigo is a false, disorienting sensation and does not help maintain balance, so E is the false statement. It results from endolymph momentum at the end of rotation, impulses reaching the superior temporal gyrus, may arise from canal or nerve irritation, and occurs in Meniere disease and motion sickness.
questions.keyConcept: Vertigo does not help maintain balance.
options: Is due to momentum of endolymph at the end of rotation
Is due to impulses that reach to the superior temporal gyrus
May be felt in absence of rotation due to irritation of SCCs or vestibular nerve
Occurs in Meniere’s disease and in motion sickness
It is important to maintain balance at the end of rotation

questions.text: Nystagmus:-
questions.explanation: Rotational nystagmus is a vestibulo-ocular reflex driven by the canals, so it occurs even in blind persons (D). It results from asymmetrical (not symmetrical) discharge, helps stabilize gaze via its slow phase, and is initiated by vestibular (not visual) impulses.
questions.keyConcept: Rotational nystagmus is a vestibulo-ocular reflex, present even in the blind.
options: Occurs as a result of symmetrical bilateral discharge from the SCCs at the onset of rotation
Occurs as a result of symmetrical bilateral discharge from the SCCs at the end of rotation
Prevents stabilization of the eye balls on visual objects
Is a vestibulo-ocular reflex occurs even in blind persons.
It is initiated by visual impulses.

questions.text: Regarding Nystagmus, all of the following are true, EXCEPT:-
questions.explanation: Nystagmus can be pathological (e.g. labyrinthine or central disease), so C is the false statement. Its slow component is opposite to rotation, it occurs at start, end, and speed change, its fast component is a reticular compensatory reflex, and it reflects asymmetrical canal discharge.
questions.keyConcept: Nystagmus can be pathological -- not always physiological.
options: Its slow component occurs in the opposite direction of rotation.
Occurs at the start, end and change in speed of rotation.
It is always a physiological phenomenon.
Its fast component is a compensatory reticular reflex.
Occurs in conditions of asymmetrical discharge from SCCs.

questions.text: Post-rotational alteration in muscle tone:-
questions.explanation: At the end of rotation the endolymph momentum reverses cupular deflection, increasing discharge from the canal on the side opposite the original rotation, which alters muscle tone (past-pointing) (D).
questions.keyConcept: Post-rotation: increased discharge from the canal opposite the rotation.
options: Results from altered pattern of macular discharge
Maintains equilibrium at the start of rotation
Results from increased discharge from the SCCs on both sides
Results from increased discharge from the SCCs on the opposite side of original rotation.
Is due to decreased activity of equilibrium center

questions.text: Regarding the macula:-
questions.explanation: The maculae can initiate postural (righting) reflexes (A). The utricular macula detects horizontal (not vertical) linear acceleration, the macula is not the canal receptor, it responds to linear acceleration and gravity (not rotation), and its otoconia are denser than the endolymph.
questions.keyConcept: The maculae can initiate postural reflexes.
options: Macula of utricle detects linear vertical acceleration.
It is the receptor of semicircular canals.
Has otoconia which has the same density as the endolymph.

questions.text: Maculae of vestibular apparatus are:-
questions.explanation: The maculae change their discharge pattern with head tilt as the dense otoconia shift and bend the hair cells (C). They are stimulated by otoconial shear (not endolymph flow over them), function in all postures, the otoconia may bend cilia toward or away from the kinocilium, and they respond to linear movement.
questions.keyConcept: The maculae change discharge with head tilt (otoconial shear).
options: Stimulated by movement of endolymph over their surface
Stimulated during standing upright but inhibited in the recumbent posture
Alter the pattern of their discharge by head tilting
Contain otoconia that press on hair cells towars the kinocilium.
Stimulated by head rotation in the vertical plane

questions.text: Momentum of the endolymph is the basis of sensing:-
questions.explanation: The momentum (inertia) of endolymph at the end of rotation deflects the cupula and produces a false sensation of rotation (post-rotational vertigo) (D).
questions.keyConcept: Endolymph momentum underlies the false sensation of rotation.
options: Head tilt from side to side

questions.text: Which of the following does NOT produce vertigo:-
questions.explanation: Among these options, simple head-bending during diving does not by itself produce vertigo, so B is the answer. Post-rotational endolymph movement, Meniere disease, motion sickness, and even refractive errors can produce vertigo or dizziness.
questions.keyConcept: Simple head-bending while diving does not produce vertigo.
options: Bending of the head during diving.

questions.text: Which of the following connections of the vestibular apparatus is responsible for inducing muscle tone changes:-
questions.explanation: Vestibular influence on muscle tone is mediated largely through the reticular formation (reticulospinal) and vestibulospinal pathways (B).
questions.keyConcept: Vestibular muscle-tone changes act via the reticular formation.

questions.text: The start of linear horizontal acceleration is associated with:-
questions.explanation: At the start of forward linear acceleration the otoconia lag backward, signaling a backward tilt, and the reflex response is leaning forward to maintain balance (E). The otoconia lag backward (not forward) by their inertia.
questions.keyConcept: Start of forward acceleration triggers a reflex leaning forward.
options: Stimulation of crista ampullaris of horizontal semicircular canals.
Falling of otolith forward by its momentum.

questions.text: At the end of a rotation to the right, Nystagmus is:-
questions.explanation: When rotation to the right stops, the reversed endolymph deflection reverses the nystagmus: the slow component now moves left-to-right (toward the right) and the fast component beats to the left (C).
questions.keyConcept: End of rightward rotation: nystagmus slow phase moves left-to-right.
options: Has a slow component from right to left.
Has a fast component from left to right.
Has a slow component from left to right.
Has slow and fast components identical to those at the start of rotation.

questions.text: Which of the following receptors is the primary one responsible for detection of head position during diving:-
questions.explanation: When visual cues are absent, as underwater, head position relative to gravity is detected primarily by the maculae of the otolith organs (D).
questions.keyConcept: Underwater, head position is detected primarily by the maculae.

questions.text: After a 30 seconds of constant speed angular acceleration to the right,:-
questions.explanation: At constant velocity the endolymph catches up with the canals, the cupula returns to rest, and both sides discharge equally, so no rotation is sensed (E).
questions.keyConcept: At constant speed both cristae discharge equally (no rotation sensed).
options: The inertia of the endolymph makes it moves to the left.
The momentum of the endolymph makes it continues to move to the right.
The right crista is stimulated, while the left is inhibited.
The left crista is stimulated, while the right is inhibited.
Cristae of both ears discharge equal impulses.

questions.text: Following angular acceleration to the right, if a person is asked to touch a point on the wall, while closing his eyes, he:-
questions.explanation: Past-pointing occurs in the direction of the preceding rotation, so after rightward rotation the person points to the right of the target (B).
questions.keyConcept: Past-pointing is in the direction of the preceding rotation (to the right).
options: Touches to the right of the point.
Touches to the left of the point.
Can not see the point because of nystagmus.

questions.text: Sweating and vomiting that associate acceleration are due to:-
questions.explanation: The autonomic accompaniments of acceleration (sweating, nausea, vomiting) are mediated by vestibular projections to the reticular formation and its autonomic centers (C).
questions.keyConcept: Sweating and vomiting with acceleration act via the reticular formation.
options: Stimulation of medial longitudinal bundles of both sides.

questions.text: List the eye layers, and the parts of each layer.
questions.keyConcept: Eye coats: fibrous (cornea + sclera), vascular uvea (iris, ciliary body, choroid), nervous (retina).
questions.modelAnswer:
The eyeball wall is formed of **three concentric coats (tunics):**

- **Outer fibrous (protective) tunic** -- tough and supportive:
	- **Cornea**: transparent anterior 1/6, the main refracting surface.
	- **Sclera**: opaque white posterior 5/6 that maintains the shape of the globe.
- **Middle vascular tunic (uvea)** -- nutritive and pigmented:
	- **Iris** (anteriorly) with the pupil.
	- **Ciliary body** (accommodation + aqueous secretion).
	- **Choroid** (posteriorly; nourishes the outer retina and absorbs stray light).
- **Inner nervous tunic (retina)**:
	- **Pigment epithelium** (outer).
	- **Neural retina** (photoreceptors and the neural layers).

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the eye contents.
questions.keyConcept: Eye contents: aqueous humor, crystalline lens, vitreous body.
questions.modelAnswer:
The transparent refractive contents (dioptric media) of the eye are:

- **Aqueous humor** -- fills the anterior and posterior chambers.
- **Crystalline lens** -- biconvex, suspended behind the iris.
- **Vitreous body (humor)** -- gel filling the large posterior cavity behind the lens.

Together with the cornea these form the refractive media of the eye.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the eye chambers, and the contents of each chamber.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior + posterior chambers hold aqueous humor; vitreous chamber holds vitreous body.
questions.modelAnswer:
| Chamber | Boundaries | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Anterior chamber** | between cornea (front) and iris (back) | aqueous humor |
| **Posterior chamber** | between iris (front) and lens/zonules (back) | aqueous humor |
| **Vitreous (postremal) chamber** | behind the lens, the largest cavity | vitreous body (humor) |

The anterior and posterior chambers communicate through the pupil.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Outline the effects of: refractive index, Angle of incidence and Degree of lens curvature on light refraction.
questions.keyConcept: Refraction increases with the difference in refractive index, the angle of incidence, and lens curvature.
questions.modelAnswer:
Refraction is the bending of light as it passes between media of different optical density:

- **Refractive index**: the greater the *difference* in refractive index between the two media, the greater the bending of light.
- **Angle of incidence**: the more oblique (larger) the angle of incidence, the greater the refraction. A ray striking the surface perpendicularly (90 degrees) passes straight through undeviated.
- **Degree of lens curvature**: the more curved (more convex) the surface, the shorter the focal length and the greater the converging (dioptric) power.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the refractive index of different eye refractive structures.
questions.keyConcept: Refractive indices: air 1.0, cornea 1.38, aqueous 1.33, lens approx 1.40, vitreous 1.34.
questions.modelAnswer:
| Medium | Refractive index |
| --- | --- |
| Air | 1.00 |
| Cornea | 1.38 |
| Aqueous humor | 1.33 |
| Crystalline lens (average) | approx 1.40 |
| Vitreous humor | 1.34 |

The largest index jump is air to cornea, so most refraction happens at the corneal surface.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Describe how the diopteric power of a lens is calculated.
questions.keyConcept: Dioptric power P = 1 / focal length in metres; converging lens positive.
questions.modelAnswer:
The refractive (dioptric) power of a lens is expressed in **diopters (D)** and equals the reciprocal of its focal length measured in **metres**:

- **P = 1 / f (metres)**
- A converging (convex) lens has a positive value; a diverging (concave) lens is negative.
- Example: a lens that focuses parallel rays at 0.1 m has a power of 1 / 0.1 = **10 D**; at 0.025 m it is 40 D.
- The total power of the resting eye is about **59 D**, of which the cornea contributes about 43 D and the lens about 15 to 20 D.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Mention the lens formula.
questions.keyConcept: Lens formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v; in the eye v is fixed so f changes (accommodation).
questions.modelAnswer:
The lens (thin lens) formula relates focal length to object and image distances:

- **1 / f = 1 / u + 1 / v**
	where f = focal length, u = object distance, v = image distance.
- In the eye the **image distance (v) is fixed** because the retina lies at a constant distance behind the lens.
- Therefore, when the object distance (u) changes, the **focal length / power of the lens must change** to keep the image focused on the retina -- this is the optical basis of **accommodation**.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Enumerate the eye protective mechanisms.
questions.keyConcept: Eye protection: orbit, eyelids/lashes, eyebrows, tears, conjunctiva, fibrous coat, protective reflexes.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Bony orbit** -- shields the globe from trauma.
- **Eyelids and eyelashes** -- blink reflex spreads tears and blocks foreign bodies.
- **Eyebrows** -- divert sweat and particles.
- **Lacrimal apparatus / tears** -- wash away debris and provide antibacterial lysozyme and IgA.
- **Conjunctiva** -- protective mucous membrane.
- **Tough fibrous coat** (cornea and sclera) -- mechanical protection.
- **Rich corneal/conjunctival pain innervation** -- triggers protective reflexes.
- **Pupillary light reflex** -- protects the retina from excess light.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the reflexes that induce eyelid closure.
questions.keyConcept: Lid closure: corneal/blink reflex, dazzle reflex, menace reflex, reflex blinking, sleep.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Corneal (blink) reflex** -- touching the cornea/conjunctiva (afferent trigeminal V, efferent facial VII).
- **Dazzle reflex** -- sudden bright light.
- **Menace (visual threat) reflex** -- an object approaching the eye.
- **Reflex (periodic) blinking** -- spreads the tear film.
- **Lid closure during sleep and on forced effort.**
- **Lacrimation/foreign body reflex** -- irritation of the ocular surface.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Give an account on the lacrimal system, its functions and abnormalities.
questions.keyConcept: Lacrimal system: gland secretes tears, drained via puncta to nasolacrimal duct; lubricates and protects.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Structure / secretory part:**
- Main **lacrimal gland** (superolateral orbit) plus accessory glands secrete tears.

**Drainage part:**
- Tears flow across the eye to the medial canthus, into the **puncta** then **canaliculi**, into the **lacrimal sac**, down the **nasolacrimal duct** to the nasal cavity.

**Functions:**
- Lubrication for lid movement, supply of oxygen and nutrients to the cornea, antibacterial action (lysozyme, IgA), washing of debris, and a smooth uniform optical surface.

**Abnormalities:**
- **Dry eye / xerophthalmia** (reduced secretion), **epiphora** (overflow tearing from blocked drainage), **dacryocystitis** (lacrimal sac infection), and reduced secretion in facial nerve lesions.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Describe the structure of tears, and list the source and importance of each component.
questions.keyConcept: Tear film: lipid (meibomian), aqueous (lacrimal gland), mucin (goblet cells).
questions.modelAnswer:
The tear film has **three layers:**

| Layer | Source | Importance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Lipid (outer)** | Meibomian (tarsal) glands | reduces evaporation, stabilises the film |
| **Aqueous (middle, thickest)** | lacrimal + accessory glands | oxygen and nutrients to cornea, lysozyme and IgA for antibacterial action, washes debris |
| **Mucin (inner)** | conjunctival goblet cells | wets the hydrophobic corneal epithelium and lets tears spread evenly |

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Enumerate functions of cornea.
questions.keyConcept: Cornea: major refraction (approx 43 D), light transmission, protection, pain sensation.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Main refractive surface** of the eye (about 43 D, roughly two-thirds of total dioptric power).
- **Transmission of light** owing to its transparency.
- **Protection** -- part of the tough fibrous coat and a barrier to microbes.
- **Sensation** -- richly innervated with pain (irritant) receptors that trigger protective blink and tearing reflexes.
- Helps **maintain the shape** of the anterior eye.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the causes of corneal transparency.
questions.keyConcept: Corneal transparency: avascular, dehydrated (Na pump), regular collagen, non-keratinised epithelium.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Avascularity** -- no blood vessels to scatter light.
- **Relative dehydration** maintained by the **Na+/K+ pumps** of the endothelium and epithelium.
- **Regular, uniform arrangement** of stromal collagen fibrils of equal small diameter.
- **Non-keratinised** surface epithelium.
- **Tight junctions** of epithelium and endothelium limit water entry.
- **Uniform refractive index** of corneal components.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the causes of corneal opacity.
questions.keyConcept: Corneal opacity: oedema (pump failure), vascularisation, scarring, inflammation, vit A deficiency.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Corneal oedema (overhydration)** from endothelial pump failure or a high intraocular pressure.
- **Vascularisation** of the normally avascular cornea.
- **Scarring** with irregular collagen after ulcers or trauma.
- **Inflammation (keratitis)** and infection.
- **Keratinisation / xerosis** as in vitamin A deficiency.
- **Deposits** (lipid, calcium) and oedema disrupting fibril spacing.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Enumerate the sources of corneal nutrition.
questions.keyConcept: Cornea fed by oxygen from tears/air, and glucose mainly from aqueous humor; limbal vessels at periphery.
questions.modelAnswer:
Because the cornea is avascular it is nourished by diffusion:

- **Oxygen** -- mainly atmospheric oxygen dissolved in the **tear film** (anterior surface), with some from the **aqueous humor** (posterior surface).
- **Glucose and nutrients** -- mainly from the **aqueous humor**.
- **Peripheral limbal blood vessels** supply the corneal margin.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Discuss the mechanisms of corneal dehydration.
questions.keyConcept: Corneal dehydration: endothelial/epithelial Na-K pumps draw water out; barriers limit entry; surface evaporation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Relative dehydration keeps the stroma transparent and is maintained by:

- **Active ion transport** -- the **Na+/K+ ATPase** of the **endothelium** (main) and epithelium pumps ions out, and **water follows osmotically** out of the stroma.
- Supporting endothelial mechanisms: **carbonic anhydrase** and **Na+/H+ exchange**.
- **Intact epithelial and endothelial barriers** (tight junctions) limit water entry.
- **Evaporation** from the anterior tear-covered surface.

Failure of the pump or barrier leads to stromal oedema and opacity.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Discuss physiology aqueous humor.
questions.keyConcept: Aqueous humor: secreted by ciliary processes, circulates to trabecular meshwork, nourishes and sets IOP.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Site:** fills the posterior and anterior chambers.
- **Formation:** by the **ciliary processes**, mainly by **active secretion** (Na+/K+ ATPase, aided by carbonic anhydrase) plus secondary active transport, diffusion and minor filtration; about 2 to 3 microlitres/min.
- **Circulation:** posterior chamber to pupil to anterior chamber to the **trabecular meshwork** to the **canal of Schlemm** to episcleral veins.
- **Functions:** nourishes the avascular cornea and lens, removes wastes, maintains **intraocular pressure** and eye shape, and is a clear refractive medium.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Outline the mechanism of formation of fluid of the anterior and posterior chambers of the eye.
questions.keyConcept: Aqueous formed by primary active Na secretion of ciliary epithelium, plus secondary transport, diffusion, filtration.
questions.modelAnswer:
Aqueous humor is formed by the **non-pigmented ciliary epithelium** through several mechanisms:

- **Primary active secretion (main):** Na+/K+ ATPase actively transports Na+; **carbonic anhydrase** generates HCO3- that is secreted.
- **Secondary active transport** of glucose and amino acids.
- **Osmosis:** water follows the secreted solutes.
- **Diffusion** of lipid-soluble substances down their gradients.
- **Ultrafiltration** from ciliary capillaries (minor contribution).

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Describe the circulation and the drainage of aqueous humor.
questions.keyConcept: Aqueous: posterior chamber to pupil to anterior chamber to trabecular meshwork to canal of Schlemm.
questions.modelAnswer:
- Secreted into the **posterior chamber**.
- Flows through the **pupil** into the **anterior chamber**.
- Reaches the **iridocorneal (anterior chamber) angle**.
- Passes through the **trabecular meshwork** into the **canal of Schlemm**.
- Drains via aqueous and episcleral veins into the venous circulation (conventional route, about 90%).
- A smaller **uveoscleral route** (about 10%) drains through the ciliary muscle.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Enumerate the functions of aqueous humor.
questions.keyConcept: Aqueous functions: nourishes cornea/lens, removes wastes, maintains IOP and shape, optical medium.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Nutrition and oxygenation** of the avascular **cornea and lens**, and removal of their metabolic wastes.
- **Maintains intraocular pressure** and the shape of the globe.
- Acts as a **clear refractive medium** in the light path.
- Helps maintain corneal and lens **transparency**.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Give an account on the intraocular pressure.
questions.keyConcept: IOP normally 12 to 20 mmHg, set by balance of aqueous formation and outflow; raised in glaucoma.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Normal value:** about **12 to 20 mmHg**, measured by tonometry.
- **Determined by** the balance between **aqueous formation** and **outflow**, with outflow resistance at the trabecular meshwork being the main regulated factor.
- **Variations:** slightly higher in the morning, and tends to rise with age and posture.
- **Importance:** maintains the shape and optical alignment of the eye and, transmitted through taut zonules, keeps the lens flattened for far vision.
- A pathological rise (impaired outflow) causes **glaucoma** and optic nerve damage.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Define glaucoma, its causes.
questions.keyConcept: Glaucoma: pathological rise in IOP from impaired aqueous outflow (open-angle or closed-angle).
questions.modelAnswer:
**Definition:** a pathological rise in intraocular pressure that damages the retina and optic nerve and can cause blindness.

**Causes (mainly impaired aqueous outflow):**
- **Open-angle (chronic):** increased resistance at the trabecular meshwork while the angle is open.
- **Closed-angle (acute):** narrowing or closure of the iridocorneal angle blocking outflow.
- **Secondary:** inflammation, trauma, lens or vascular disease.
- Rarely, **excessive aqueous formation.**

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the effects and treatment of glaucoma.
questions.keyConcept: Glaucoma: optic damage, field loss, blindness, lost accommodation; treat by lowering IOP, avoid atropine.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Effects:**
- Optic disc cupping, retinal ganglion cell damage, progressive **visual field loss** and eventual **blindness**.
- **Loss of accommodation**; pain and halos in acute attacks; symptoms worsened by pupillary dilatation.

**Treatment (lower the intraocular pressure):**
- **Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors** and beta-blockers/prostaglandins to reduce formation.
- **Miotics (pilocarpine, a parasympathomimetic)** to open the angle and improve outflow.
- **Laser or surgery** (trabeculoplasty, iridotomy).
- **Avoid atropine and mydriatics**, which can precipitate angle closure.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Describe the structure and functions of the crystalline lens.
questions.keyConcept: Lens: biconvex, avascular, no nerves; refracts and accommodates; held by zonules.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Structure:**
- **Biconvex, transparent, avascular** with **no nerve supply**.
- Covered by an elastic **capsule**, with an anterior **epithelium** and **lens fibres** forming a cortex and a denser nucleus.
- Suspended by **suspensory ligaments (zonules)** attached to the ciliary body.

**Functions:**
- Contributes **refractive power** (about 15 to 20 D at rest).
- **Accommodation** -- changes its convexity to focus near objects.
- Helps **absorb ultraviolet** light.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the causes of lens transparency.
questions.keyConcept: Lens transparency: avascular, regular fibres, high glutathione, ion pumps maintain dehydration.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Avascularity.**
- **Regular, ordered arrangement** of lens fibres, which lose their organelles when mature.
- High content of **glutathione** (antioxidant) preventing protein denaturation.
- **Na+/K+ and Ca++ pumps** maintain ionic and osmotic balance (relative dehydration).
- A **semipermeable capsule** controlling water and solute movement.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Write short notes about cataract.
questions.keyConcept: Cataract: lens opacity from ageing, UV, diabetes, trauma; causes painless visual loss; treated surgically.
questions.modelAnswer:
- **Definition:** opacity (loss of transparency) of the crystalline lens.
- **Causes:** ageing (senile), ultraviolet exposure, **diabetes** (sorbitol/osmotic water entry), trauma, congenital, corticosteroids; underlying mechanisms are **denaturation of lens proteins**, a fall in protective **glutathione**, and osmotic swelling.
- **Effects:** progressive, painless blurring of vision and glare.
- **Treatment:** surgical removal of the opaque lens with insertion of an intraocular lens.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Define the near response and list its components.
questions.keyConcept: Near response (triad): accommodation, convergence, and miosis when viewing a near object.
questions.modelAnswer:
**Definition:** the set of automatic adjustments that occur when gaze shifts from a far to a near object so that a clear single image is kept on both foveae.

**Components (the near triad):**
- **Accommodation** -- increased convexity and power of the lens.
- **Convergence** -- both eyes turn inward (medial recti).
- **Miosis** -- constriction of the pupils.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*
