questions.text: Describe the ability of a normal person to use both eyes to perceive one visual image (Binocular vision).
questions.keyConcept: Binocular vision: images on corresponding retinal points are fused in the cortex into one image with stereoscopic depth.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Binocular vision

- Each eye sees a slightly different image of the same object.
- When these images fall on **corresponding retinal points**, they are **fused by the visual cortex into a single image**.
- The small disparity between the two images gives **stereoscopic (3D) depth perception**.
- It also widens the total field and compensates for each eye's blind spot.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the requirements of binocular vision.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory: clear similar images on corresponding points, intact pathway/cortex. Motor: balanced extraocular muscles.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Requirements of binocular vision

**Sensory requirements:**
- Clear images of **similar size and clarity** in each eye.
- Images falling on **corresponding retinal points**.
- Intact **visual pathways and cortex** for fusion.

**Motor requirements:**
- **Balanced, coordinated extraocular muscles** that keep both visual axes aligned on the target.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Outline the development of binocular vision.
questions.keyConcept: Binocular vision develops after birth with normal visual experience; matures gradually, complete by about 6 years.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Development of binocular vision

- It is **not present at birth** but develops during infancy and childhood.
- It **requires normal visual experience** from both eyes during the critical period.
- It matures **gradually** and is **complete by about 6 years** of age.
- Deprivation (e.g. uncorrected squint or refractive error) in this period leads to **amblyopia**.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Outline the grades of binocular vision.
questions.keyConcept: Three grades (Worth): simultaneous perception, fusion, and stereopsis (3D depth perception).
questions.modelAnswer:
### Grades of binocular vision (Worth classification)

1. **Simultaneous perception:** both eyes perceive their images at the same time.
2. **Fusion:** the two images are blended into one.
3. **Stereopsis:** appreciation of **three-dimensional depth** from retinal disparity (the highest grade).

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Outline the advantages of binocular vision.
questions.keyConcept: Single fused image, wider field, stereoscopic depth, compensates blind spot, masks a minor defect in one eye.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Advantages of binocular vision

- A **single, fused image** despite two eyes.
- A **wider total visual field**.
- **Stereoscopic (3D) depth perception** and better distance judgment.
- **Compensation for the blind spot** of each eye.
- **Masking of a minor defect** in one eye by the other.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Give an account on after image.
questions.keyConcept: After image: visual sensation persisting after stimulus removed; positive (same color, brief), negative (complementary).
questions.modelAnswer:
### After image

An **after image** is a visual sensation that persists after the stimulus is removed.
- **Positive after image:** of the **same color** as the stimulus, very brief, due to continued receptor discharge.
- **Negative after image:** of the **complementary color**, lasting longer, due to **adaptation/bleaching** of the cones that were stimulated, so the opponent color dominates.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Discuss the terms flicker and critical fusion frequency.
questions.keyConcept: Flicker: perceiving intermittent light as flickering; CFF: frequency above which flashes fuse to steady light
questions.modelAnswer:
### Flicker and critical fusion frequency

- **Flicker:** when a light is interrupted at a low rate, it is perceived as flickering (on-off).
- **Critical fusion frequency (CFF):** the frequency above which the separate flashes **fuse into a steady, continuous light**.
- CFF is about **50-60 per second** and **increases with light intensity**.
- It is the basis of **cinema and television**, where rapid frames appear as continuous motion.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Define squint and describe its effects.
questions.keyConcept: Squint (strabismus): misaligned visual axes; causes diplopia and confusion; in children leads to amblyopia ex anopsia.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Squint (strabismus)

**Definition:** misalignment of the visual axes, so the two eyes do not point at the same object.

**Effects:**
- **Diplopia** (double vision) because images fall on non-corresponding points.
- **Visual confusion** (two different images superimposed).
- In **children**, the cortex **suppresses** the image of the deviating eye to avoid diplopia; if untreated this becomes permanent **amblyopia ex anopsia** (lazy eye).

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List types of eye movements.
questions.keyConcept: Saccades, smooth pursuit, vergence (convergence/divergence), vestibulo-ocular reflex, and optokinetic movements.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Types of eye movements

- **Saccades:** rapid, jerky shifts of gaze between targets.
- **Smooth pursuit:** slow tracking of a moving object.
- **Vergence:** convergence and divergence to fixate near or far objects (disjunctive).
- **Vestibulo-ocular reflex:** stabilizes gaze during head movement.
- **Optokinetic movements:** follow a moving scene then reset.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List components and functions of the external ear.
questions.keyConcept: External ear: pinna and external auditory canal; collects/funnels sound, aids localization, resonance, protects drum.
questions.modelAnswer:
### External ear

**Components:** the **pinna (auricle)** and the **external auditory canal**, ending at the tympanic membrane.

**Functions:**
- **Collects and funnels** sound waves toward the tympanic membrane.
- Aids **sound localization** (especially in the vertical plane).
- Provides **resonance** that amplifies speech frequencies (around 3000 Hz).
- **Protects** the tympanic membrane (hair, wax, and the canal's shape).

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Describe parts and characters of external auditory canal.
questions.keyConcept: Canal ~2.5 cm, S-shaped: outer third cartilaginous with hair and ceruminous glands, inner two-thirds bony and bare.
questions.modelAnswer:
### External auditory canal

- About **2.5 cm** long and **S-shaped**.
- **Outer one-third: cartilaginous**, lined by skin bearing **hair and ceruminous (wax) glands**.
- **Inner two-thirds: bony**, with thin skin and **no hair or glands**.
- Self-cleaning (wax and epithelial migration), and acts as a **resonator** (around 3000 Hz) that amplifies sound before it reaches the drum.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Describe the structure and size of the tympanic membrane.
questions.keyConcept: Drum: thin oval cone ~9x10 mm, ~55 mm2 effective area; three layers; umbo at apex attached to malleus handle.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Tympanic membrane (eardrum)

**Size:** a thin, semi-transparent, oval, slightly **cone-shaped** membrane, about **9 x 10 mm**, with an effective vibrating area of about **55 mm2**.

**Structure (three layers):**
- Outer: skin (continuous with the canal).
- Middle: fibrous (radial and circular fibres) giving tension.
- Inner: mucous membrane (continuous with the middle ear).

The apex of the cone (the **umbo**) is attached to the handle of the **malleus**.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the functions of the tympanic membrane and explain its adaptations to its function.
questions.keyConcept: Drum converts sound to ossicular vibration; aperiodic and highly damped for faithful, distortion-free reproduction.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Functions and adaptations of the tympanic membrane

**Function:** converts sound-wave pressure into **mechanical vibrations** transmitted to the ossicles, and helps in impedance matching.

**Adaptations:**
- **Aperiodic:** has no natural resonant frequency of its own, so it **faithfully reproduces** any incoming sound.
- **Highly damped:** stops vibrating **immediately** when the sound ends, with no after-vibration, preventing distortion.
- **Cone shape and fibrous tension** allow efficient, sensitive transfer of energy to the malleus.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Outline the contents of the middle ear. Enumerate the function of each.
questions.keyConcept: Middle ear: air, ossicles (transmit/amplify), muscles (attenuate), Eustachian tube (pressure), oval/round windows.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Contents of the middle ear and their functions

| Content | Function |
|---|---|
| Air | Allows free vibration of the drum and ossicles; equalizes pressure |
| Ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes) | Transmit and amplify sound to the oval window (impedance matching) |
| Tensor tympani and stapedius muscles | Attenuation reflex protecting against loud sound |
| Opening of the Eustachian tube | Equalizes middle-ear pressure with the atmosphere |
| Oval and round windows | Couple the ossicles to the cochlear fluid and relieve pressure |

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Explain the source of air present in the middle ear, and list its importance.
questions.keyConcept: Air enters via the Eustachian tube from the nasopharynx; equalizes pressure across the drum for free vibration.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Source and importance of middle-ear air

**Source:** air reaches the middle ear from the **nasopharynx through the Eustachian tube**.

**Importance:**
- **Equalizes pressure** on both sides of the tympanic membrane so it can **vibrate freely**.
- Allows **free movement of the ossicles**.
- Prevents **retraction or distortion** of the drum and the conductive hearing loss that follows pressure imbalance.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Give an account on: names, articulation and connections of the bony ossicles.
questions.keyConcept: Malleus, incus, stapes form a chain; malleus to drum, articulate by synovial joints, stapes footplate in oval window.
questions.modelAnswer:
### The bony ossicles

**Names (lateral to medial):** **malleus** (hammer), **incus** (anvil), **stapes** (stirrup).

**Connections and articulation:**
- The **handle of the malleus** is attached to the tympanic membrane (umbo).
- The malleus **articulates with the incus** by a synovial joint.
- The incus **articulates with the stapes**.
- The **footplate of the stapes** fits into the **oval window**, held by the annular ligament.

Together they form a **lever (ossicular) chain** transmitting vibration from drum to cochlea.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Describe how the bony ossicles amplify sound vibrations.
questions.keyConcept: Lever action (~1.3x) plus tympanic-to-oval-window area ratio (~17x) give about 22-fold pressure gain.
questions.modelAnswer:
### How the ossicles amplify sound

1. **Lever action:** the malleus arm is longer than the incus arm, giving about **1.3-fold** force gain.
2. **Area (hydraulic) ratio:** the effective tympanic membrane area is about **17 times larger** than the stapes footplate (oval window), so force is concentrated onto a smaller area, multiplying pressure ~17-fold.

The combined effect is about a **22-fold** increase in pressure, which overcomes the high impedance of the cochlear fluid.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Explain the phenomenon of “impedance matching” of boney ossicles.
questions.keyConcept: Impedance matching: ossicular lever + area ratio raise pressure ~22x so air-borne sound transfers into cochlear fluid.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Impedance matching

- Sound passing directly from **air to the dense cochlear fluid** would have most of its energy (about 99.9%) **reflected** because of the impedance mismatch.
- The **ossicular system** overcomes this by raising the **pressure** about 22-fold (lever action ~1.3x and area ratio ~17x).
- This **matches the low impedance of air to the high impedance of the cochlear fluid**, so sound energy is transferred efficiently rather than reflected.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Describe the middle ear muscles and outline their role in hearing.
questions.keyConcept: Tensor tympani (V) and stapedius (VII) contract reflexly to stiffen the chain and attenuate loud, low-frequency sound.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Middle-ear muscles

- **Tensor tympani:** attached to the malleus, supplied by the **trigeminal nerve**; pulls the drum inward.
- **Stapedius:** attached to the stapes, supplied by the **facial nerve**; pulls the stapes.

**Role:** they contract reflexly to loud sound (the **attenuation/acoustic reflex**), **stiffening the ossicular chain** and reducing transmission of loud, low-frequency sound. This **protects the inner ear**, reduces masking of higher frequencies, and attenuates one's own voice during speech.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Give an account on the tympanic attenuation acoustic reflex.
questions.keyConcept: Acoustic reflex: bilateral stapedius/tensor tympani contraction to loud sound (>70-90 dB); latency 40-160 ms.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Tympanic attenuation (acoustic) reflex

- A **bilateral reflex contraction** of the **stapedius and tensor tympani** in response to **loud sound** (about 70-90 dB and above).
- **Latency 40-160 ms**, so it **cannot protect against very sudden** loud sounds (gunshots, explosions).
- **Functions:** protect the inner ear from sustained loud sound, reduce masking of important (higher) frequencies, and attenuate the sound of one's own voice during speaking and singing.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Write short notes on the Eustachian tube and its role in hearing.
questions.keyConcept: Eustachian tube (~3.5 cm) links nasopharynx to middle ear; opens on swallowing to equalize pressure across the drum.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Eustachian tube

- A tube about **3.5 cm** long connecting the **nasopharynx to the middle ear**.
- Normally **closed**, it opens during **swallowing, yawning and chewing**.

**Role in hearing:**
- **Equalizes** middle-ear pressure with the atmosphere across the tympanic membrane, keeping it freely mobile.
- **Drains** middle-ear secretions.
- Dysfunction causes drum retraction, **conductive hearing loss**, and predisposes to middle-ear infection.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Describe what happens to hearing during ascent and descent of an airplane. Explain your answer.
questions.keyConcept: Ascent: middle-ear pressure exceeds outside, drum bulges, tube vents easily. Descent: outside higher, drum retracts
questions.modelAnswer:
### Hearing during airplane ascent and descent

- **Ascent:** atmospheric pressure **falls**, so middle-ear pressure becomes **higher** than outside; the drum **bulges outward** and the Eustachian tube opens easily to vent air (mild popping, quickly relieved).
- **Descent:** atmospheric pressure **rises**, so the outside pressure is **higher** than the middle ear; the tube tends to stay **closed**, the drum is **retracted**, and hearing becomes **muffled with discomfort** until swallowing opens the tube and equalizes pressure.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Describe what happens to hearing during common cold. Explain your answer.
questions.keyConcept: Cold blocks the Eustachian tube; trapped air absorbed gives negative pressure, drum retracts, conductive hearing loss.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Hearing during a common cold

- Nasopharyngeal **congestion and swelling block the Eustachian tube**.
- The **trapped middle-ear air is gradually absorbed**, producing **negative pressure**.
- The tympanic membrane is **retracted** and its mobility reduced, causing a **conductive hearing loss** with a sensation of fullness.
- Fluid may accumulate (effusion) and infection may follow (otitis media).

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the situations where the Eustachian tube opens automatically.
questions.keyConcept: Opens on swallowing, yawning, chewing, sneezing, Valsalva, and ascent in an airplane.
questions.modelAnswer:
### When the Eustachian tube opens automatically

- **Swallowing**
- **Yawning**
- **Chewing**
- **Sneezing**
- **Forced expiration against a closed nose and mouth (Valsalva)**
- **Ascent in an airplane** (when middle-ear pressure exceeds atmospheric)

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the physiological and the pathological routes of sound transmission to the inner ear. Which route is preferred? Explain your answer.
questions.keyConcept: Physiological: air/ossicular route (preferred, impedance matched). Pathological: bone conduction and round-window route.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Routes of sound transmission to the inner ear

**Physiological (ossicular/air route):** external canal to tympanic membrane to ossicles to oval window to cochlear fluid.

**Pathological routes:**
- **Bone conduction:** skull vibrations transmitted directly to the cochlea.
- **Air conduction directly to the round window**, bypassing the ossicles.

**Preferred route:** the **ossicular (air) route**, because the ossicles provide **impedance matching** (about 22-fold pressure gain), giving the most efficient energy transfer into the cochlear fluid. The other routes lack this amplification and are far less efficient.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Describe the structure of the cochlea.
questions.keyConcept: Spiral bony canal (~2.75 turns) round modiolus; three perilymph/endolymph scalae; organ of Corti on basilar membrane.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Structure of the cochlea

- A **spiral bony canal** of about **2.75 turns** coiled around a central pillar, the **modiolus**.
- Divided lengthwise by two membranes into **three fluid-filled compartments (scalae)**:
  - **Scala vestibuli** (perilymph, upper), beginning at the **oval window**.
  - **Scala media (cochlear duct)** (endolymph, middle).
  - **Scala tympani** (perilymph, lower), ending at the **round window**.
- Scala vestibuli and tympani communicate at the apex through the **helicotrema**.
- The **basilar membrane** carries the **organ of Corti** (hair cells with the overlying tectorial membrane), the receptor organ of hearing.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List and describe the membranes and the cavities of the cochlea.
questions.keyConcept: Membranes: basilar, Reissner, tectorial. Cavities: scala vestibuli, scala media (endolymph), scala tympani (perilymph).
questions.modelAnswer:
### Membranes and cavities of the cochlea

**Membranes:**
- **Basilar membrane:** separates scala media from scala tympani and carries the organ of Corti; narrow and stiff at the base, wide and floppy at the apex.
- **Reissner (vestibular) membrane:** separates scala media from scala vestibuli.
- **Tectorial membrane:** a gelatinous flap overlying the hair cells.

**Cavities (scalae):**
- **Scala vestibuli:** perilymph (high Na).
- **Scala media (cochlear duct):** endolymph (high K, +80 mV).
- **Scala tympani:** perilymph; joins scala vestibuli at the helicotrema.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Compare between the inner and the outer cochlear hair cells.
questions.keyConcept: Inner: single row, mainly afferent, true receptors. Outer: three rows, mainly efferent, electromotile cochlear
questions.modelAnswer:
### Inner versus outer hair cells

| Feature | Inner hair cells | Outer hair cells |
|---|---|---|
| Rows / number | Single row, ~3500 | Three rows, ~12000-20000 |
| Shape | Flask-shaped | Cylindrical |
| Innervation | Mainly afferent (~90-95% of cochlear nerve fibres) | Mainly efferent |
| Function | The true sensory receptors of hearing | Electromotile cochlear amplifier: sharpen tuning and boost sensitivity |

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the mechanism of hearing and explain the transmission of sound to the inner ear.
questions.keyConcept: Sound to drum to ossicles to oval window to perilymph travelling wave to basilar membrane to hair cells to nerve.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Mechanism of hearing and transmission of sound

**Steps of hearing:** sound collection to transmission to transduction to neural coding to perception.

**Transmission to the inner ear:**
1. Sound waves pass the external canal and vibrate the **tympanic membrane**.
2. The **ossicles** transmit and amplify the vibration (impedance matching), and the **stapes** pushes the **oval window**.
3. This sets up **pressure (travelling) waves** in the **perilymph of the scala vestibuli**, passing to the scala tympani.
4. The waves displace the **basilar membrane**, stimulating the hair cells of the organ of Corti.
5. The **round window** bulges outward to relieve the pressure.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the mechanism of hearing and explain the stimulation of cochlear receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Basilar/tectorial shearing bends stereocilia, opens K channels, K influx from endolymph depolarizes hair cell, releases
questions.modelAnswer:
### Stimulation of the cochlear receptors

1. The travelling wave displaces the **basilar membrane**, causing relative (shearing) movement between it and the **tectorial membrane**.
2. This **bends the stereocilia** of the hair cells.
3. Bending **toward the tallest stereocilium** opens **mechanically gated K+ channels** (via tip links).
4. **K+ flows in from the high-K endolymph** (driven by the endocochlear potential), **depolarizing** the hair cell.
5. Depolarization opens **Ca2+ channels**, triggering **transmitter (glutamate) release** onto cochlear-nerve endings, which fire action potentials.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Explain sound transduction.
questions.keyConcept: Mechanoelectrical transduction: stereocilia deflection opens tip-link K channels; K influx depolarizes; Ca triggers
questions.modelAnswer:
### Sound (mechanoelectrical) transduction

- Deflection of the stereocilia **toward the tallest** stretches the **tip links**, opening mechanically gated **K+ channels**.
- **K+ enters from the endolymph** (high K, +80 mV), **depolarizing** the hair cell.
- Depolarization opens voltage-gated **Ca2+ channels**, causing **glutamate release** and afferent firing.
- Deflection in the opposite direction **closes** the channels and **hyperpolarizes** the cell.

Thus mechanical movement is converted into an electrical and then a neural signal.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the mechanism of hearing and draw the auditory pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Hair cells to spiral ganglion to cochlear nuclei to superior olive to lateral lemniscus to inferior colliculus to MGB
questions.modelAnswer:
### The auditory pathway

Hair cells of the organ of Corti to spiral ganglion to:

**Cochlear nerve to Cochlear nuclei (medulla) to Superior olivary nucleus (largely crossed) to Lateral lemniscus to Inferior colliculus to Medial geniculate body to Auditory radiation to Primary auditory cortex (areas 41 and 42, superior temporal gyrus).**

Because of partial crossing at several levels, each cortex receives input from **both ears**, so a one-sided central lesion does not cause complete deafness.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Describe the functions of auditory cortical areas.
questions.keyConcept: Primary cortex (41,42): perceive pitch/loudness, tonotopy, discrimination. Association (22): interpret sound and
questions.modelAnswer:
### Functions of the auditory cortical areas

**Primary auditory cortex (areas 41 and 42):**
- Conscious **perception of sound**, its **pitch (tonotopic map)** and **loudness**.
- Discrimination of **frequency and sound patterns** and the **timing/rhythm** of sounds.
- Contributes to **localization** of the sound source.

**Auditory association cortex (Wernicke, area 22):**
- **Interpretation and recognition** of sounds and **understanding of spoken language**; **auditory memory**.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the steps of hearing mechanism and discuss cochlear potentials.
questions.keyConcept: Endocochlear +80 mV, hair-cell -60 mV, cochlear microphonic (AC mirrors sound), summating potential, then nerve action
questions.modelAnswer:
### Cochlear potentials

After the steps of hearing (transmission, basilar-membrane movement, hair-cell stimulation), several electrical potentials are recorded:
- **Endocochlear potential:** a steady **+80 mV** in the endolymph of scala media, produced by the **stria vascularis** (K+ pump). With the hair-cell resting potential (about -60 mV) it gives a large driving force (~140-150 mV).
- **Cochlear microphonic potential:** an **alternating (AC)** potential generated mainly by **outer hair cells** that faithfully **reproduces the waveform** of the sound.
- **Summating potential:** a **DC** shift during stimulation.
- **Action potentials:** in the cochlear nerve, the coded output to the brain.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Discuss the mechanism of stimulation of auditory hair cells.
questions.keyConcept: Basilar-tectorial shearing bends stereocilia, opens tip-link K channels; K influx from endolymph depolarizes, Ca
questions.modelAnswer:
### Mechanism of stimulation of auditory hair cells

1. Movement of the **basilar membrane** produces **shearing** against the overlying **tectorial membrane**.
2. The **stereocilia** of the hair cells are **bent**.
3. Bending toward the tallest stereocilium stretches **tip links** and opens **K+ channels**.
4. **K+ enters from the endolymph** (driven by the +80 mV endocochlear potential plus the negative intracellular potential), **depolarizing** the cell.
5. **Ca2+ entry** then triggers **transmitter release** onto the cochlear nerve. Bending the other way closes the channels and hyperpolarizes the cell.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Outline the functions of the olivo-cochlear bundle.
questions.keyConcept: Efferent fibers to (mainly outer) hair cells; inhibitory; reduce gain, sharpen tuning, protect from noise, aid hearing
questions.modelAnswer:
### Functions of the olivo-cochlear bundle

The olivo-cochlear bundle is an **efferent (descending)** pathway from the **superior olivary complex** to the cochlea (mainly the **outer hair cells**). It is **inhibitory (cholinergic)** and:
- **Reduces the gain/sensitivity** of the cochlear amplifier.
- **Sharpens frequency selectivity (tuning)**.
- **Protects** the cochlea from loud noise.
- Improves **detection of signals in background noise** and contributes to **selective auditory attention**.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Define: endocochlear potential and cochlear microphonic potential.
questions.keyConcept: Endocochlear potential: +80 mV of endolymph from stria vascularis. Microphonic: AC potential from hair cells mirroring
questions.modelAnswer:
### Definitions

- **Endocochlear potential:** the **+80 mV positive potential** of the **endolymph** in the scala media (relative to perilymph), produced by **K+ secretion from the stria vascularis**. It provides much of the driving force for hair-cell transduction.
- **Cochlear microphonic potential:** an **alternating (AC) electrical potential**, generated mainly by the **outer hair cells**, that faithfully **reproduces the waveform** of the sound stimulus.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Explain the ability of the auditory cortex to discriminate different sound characters (sound discrimination).
questions.keyConcept: Cortex codes pitch (tonotopy/place), loudness (rate/number of fibers), timbre (harmonics) and direction (interaural
questions.modelAnswer:
### Sound discrimination by the auditory cortex

The cortex distinguishes the characters of sound by separate codes:
- **Pitch (frequency):** place coding (tonotopic map; high at base, low at apex) plus temporal (volley) coding for low frequencies.
- **Loudness (intensity):** increased **firing rate** and **recruitment of more fibres**.
- **Timbre (quality):** the pattern of **harmonics/overtones**.
- **Direction:** interaural **time and intensity differences**.
- **Rhythm/duration:** temporal pattern of firing.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Explain how sound frequency is determined.
questions.keyConcept: High frequencies by place (base of basilar membrane); low frequencies by temporal/volley firing in phase with the wave.
questions.modelAnswer:
### How sound frequency is determined

Two complementary mechanisms code frequency (pitch):
- **Place principle:** each frequency maximally vibrates a **specific point** on the basilar membrane (**high frequency near the base, low near the apex**); the cortex reads which fibres are active. Dominant for **high frequencies**.
- **Frequency (temporal/volley) principle:** nerve fibres fire **in phase** with the sound wave; groups fire in volleys for rates the single fibre cannot follow. Dominant for **low frequencies (below about 1000-4000 Hz)**.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Outline the place theory of sound frequency discrimination.
questions.keyConcept: Place theory: each frequency peaks at a specific basilar-membrane point (high=base, low=apex), giving a tonotopic code.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Place theory

- Each sound frequency produces **maximal vibration at a particular point** along the basilar membrane.
- **High frequencies** peak near the stiff, narrow **base**; **low frequencies** peak near the wide, floppy **apex**.
- The hair cells at that point stimulate **specific nerve fibres** that project to a **tonotopic map** in the cortex, which interprets the location as a particular **pitch**.
- It best explains discrimination of **high frequencies**.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Outline the travelling wave theory of sound frequency discrimination.
questions.keyConcept: Von Bekesy: a wave travels base to apex, growing to a peak at the frequency-matched point, then dies; peak place codes
questions.modelAnswer:
### Travelling wave theory (von Bekesy)

- A sound sets up a **travelling wave** that moves along the basilar membrane **from base toward apex**.
- Its amplitude **increases** to a **peak at the point that matches the sound frequency** (resonance), then **rapidly dies out** beyond it.
- The **position of the peak depends on frequency** (base for high, apex for low), stimulating the hair cells there.
- It thus provides the physical basis of the **place code** for pitch.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Discuss the mechanism by which the auditory cortex can localize the source of a sound.
questions.keyConcept: Localization uses interaural time (phase) difference for low and interaural intensity (head shadow) for high
questions.modelAnswer:
### Localization of a sound source

The brain compares the inputs to the **two ears**:
- **Interaural time (phase) difference:** sound reaches the nearer ear slightly **earlier**; used mainly for **low frequencies**.
- **Interaural intensity difference:** the head casts a **sound shadow**, so the nearer ear hears it **louder**; used mainly for **high frequencies**.

These differences are first analysed in the **superior olivary nuclei**. The **pinna** helps localization in the **vertical plane**.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Discuss the mechanism by which the auditory cortex can discriminate the intensity of a sound.
questions.keyConcept: Loudness coded by higher firing rate, recruitment of more fibers, and activation of high-threshold fibers
questions.modelAnswer:
### Discrimination of sound intensity (loudness)

A louder sound is coded by:
- An **increased firing rate** in each active nerve fibre.
- **Recruitment of more nerve fibres** as more hair cells are stimulated.
- Activation of **high-threshold fibres** that respond only to loud sounds.

The relationship is roughly **logarithmic**, giving a very wide dynamic range; the cortex interprets the combined signal as loudness.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Define deafness, its types and causes.
questions.keyConcept: Deafness: hearing loss; conductive (external/middle ear) or sensorineural (cochlea/nerve), or mixed.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Deafness

**Definition:** partial or complete loss of hearing.

**Types and causes:**
| Type | Site | Causes |
|---|---|---|
| Conductive | External or middle ear | Wax, foreign body, perforated drum, otitis media, otosclerosis, Eustachian-tube block |
| Sensorineural | Cochlea, nerve, or central pathway | Loud noise, ototoxic drugs, presbycusis (ageing), infections, acoustic neuroma |
| Mixed | Both | Combination of the above |

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the different tests used in is diagnosis of deafness.
questions.keyConcept: Tuning-fork tests (Rinne, Weber), pure-tone and speech audiometry, tympanometry, otoacoustic emissions, BERA.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Tests for deafness

- **Tuning-fork tests:** Rinne, Weber, and Schwabach (separate conductive from sensorineural loss).
- **Pure-tone audiometry** (air and bone conduction thresholds).
- **Speech audiometry**.
- **Tympanometry / impedance audiometry** (middle-ear function and the acoustic reflex).
- **Otoacoustic emissions** (outer hair-cell function; newborn screening).
- **Brainstem evoked response audiometry (BERA)**.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Explain the effects of common cold, ascending or descending in an aircraft on hearing.
questions.keyConcept: All act via the Eustachian tube; blockage or pressure imbalance retracts the drum, causing conductive hearing loss.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Effects on hearing via the Eustachian tube

- **Common cold:** nasopharyngeal swelling **blocks the Eustachian tube**; trapped air is absorbed, producing **negative middle-ear pressure**, drum retraction, and a **conductive hearing loss** with fullness.
- **Aircraft ascent:** outside pressure falls, so middle-ear pressure is **higher**; the drum bulges and the tube **vents easily** (popping, quickly relieved).
- **Aircraft descent:** outside pressure rises and is **higher** than the middle ear; the tube tends to stay **closed**, the drum is **retracted**, and hearing is **muffled with pain** until swallowing equalizes pressure.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Why nasal drops, that decrease naso-pharynx congestion, may be used in hearing problems?
questions.keyConcept: Decongestant drops reopen the Eustachian tube, restoring middle-ear ventilation and pressure, relieving conductive loss.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Why decongestant nasal drops help hearing

- The **Eustachian tube** opens into the nasopharynx; congestion there blocks it.
- **Decongestant nasal drops reduce the nasopharyngeal/tubal swelling**, **reopening the Eustachian tube**.
- This **restores middle-ear ventilation and pressure equalization**, relieving drum retraction, fluid, and the resulting **conductive hearing loss and fullness**.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the basic taste modalities, site of their receptors on the tongue and the mechanism of stimulation of each type of receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Five tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami; salt/sour via ion channels, sweet/bitter/umami via GPCRs.

| Taste | Classic site | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| Sweet | Tip | T1R2+T1R3 GPCR to gustducin to TRPM5 to depolarization |
| Salty | Anterior sides | Na+ enters via ENaC channels to depolarization |

| Bitter | Posterior | T2R GPCR to gustducin to TRPM5 to depolarization |

The classic map overlaps; all tastes can be sensed over most of the tongue.

questions.text: Describe the site, stimuli and the mechanism of stimulation of sweet receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Sweet: classically tip; stimuli sugars/sweeteners; T1R2+T1R3 GPCR to gustducin to PLC to Ca to TRPM5 depolarization.

### Sweet receptors

- **Site:** over the tongue, classically the **tip**.
- **Stimuli:** sugars, some amino acids, and artificial sweeteners.
- **Mechanism:** the substance binds the **T1R2+T1R3 GPCR**, activating **gustducin to phospholipase C to IP3 to Ca2+ release**, which opens **TRPM5** channels, **depolarizing** the cell and releasing transmitter (ATP).

questions.text: Describe the site, stimuli and the mechanism of stimulation of salt receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Salt: anterior sides; stimulus Na+; Na enters directly through ENaC (amiloride-sensitive) channels causing

### Salt receptors

- **Site:** over the tongue, classically the **anterior sides**.
- **Stimulus:** **Na+** (sodium salts; other cations contribute).
- **Mechanism:** Na+ enters the receptor cell **directly through ENaC (amiloride-sensitive) cation channels**, **depolarizing** it and triggering transmitter release. No second messenger is needed.

questions.text: Describe the site, stimuli and the mechanism of stimulation of sour receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Sour: sides; stimulus H+ (acids); H+ enters/blocks channels (PKD2L1) depolarizing the cell.

- **Mechanism:** H+ acts on the receptor cell by **entering through proton channels (e.g. PKD2L1) and blocking K+ channels**, which **depolarizes** the cell and releases transmitter.

questions.text: Describe the site, stimuli and the mechanism of stimulation of bitter receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Bitter: posterior tongue; stimuli alkaloids/toxins; T2R GPCRs to gustducin to TRPM5 depolarization; protective.

### Bitter receptors

- **Site:** classically the **posterior (back)** of the tongue.
- **Stimuli:** **alkaloids and many toxins** (e.g. quinine), so bitterness is **protective**, provoking rejection.
- **Mechanism:** the substance binds **T2R GPCRs**, activating **gustducin to PLC to IP3 to Ca2+** and opening **TRPM5** channels, **depolarizing** the cell.

questions.text: Describe the site, stimuli and the mechanism of stimulation of umami receptors.

questions.text: List taste abnormalities.

| Feature | Taste receptors | Olfactory receptors |

| Structure | **Modified epithelial cells** (not neurons) | **True bipolar neurons** |

questions.text: Describe the mechanism of stimulation of olfactory receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Odorant binds cilia GPCR to Golf to adenylate cyclase to cAMP opens cation channels, depolarizing the olfactory neuron.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Stimulation of olfactory receptors

1. The **odorant dissolves in the mucus** covering the olfactory epithelium.
2. It **binds a GPCR** on the cilia of the olfactory receptor neuron.
3. This activates **G-protein (Golf) to adenylate cyclase**, raising **cAMP**.
4. cAMP opens **cyclic-nucleotide-gated cation channels**, letting **Na+ and Ca2+** in.
5. The cell **depolarizes** and fires **action potentials** along the olfactory nerve to the olfactory bulb.

questions.text: Describe the characters of adequate stimulus for olfactory receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Odorant must be volatile, water-soluble and lipid-soluble, and present in sufficient concentration.

### Characters of the adequate stimulus for smell

To stimulate olfactory receptors, a substance must be:
- **Volatile:** able to evaporate and reach the nose in inspired air.
- **Water-soluble:** to dissolve in the mucus layer covering the receptors.
- **Lipid-soluble:** to cross the lipid membrane of the cilia.
- Present in **sufficient concentration** (above threshold).

questions.text: Explain the rapid adaptation of smell receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Smell adapts fast (~50% in first second); partly receptor (Ca-calmodulin feedback) but mainly central habituation.

### Rapid adaptation of smell

- Olfactory sensation adapts **quickly**, falling by about **50% in the first second** and then more slowly, so a constant odor is soon no longer noticed.
- It is partly **receptor (peripheral) adaptation:** Ca2+-calmodulin feedback closes the cyclic-nucleotide-gated channels.
- It is **mainly central (CNS) habituation** within the olfactory pathway.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the olfactory disorders.
questions.keyConcept: Anosmia (loss), hyposmia (reduced), hyperosmia (increased), parosmia/dysosmia (distorted), phantosmia (hallucination).

### Olfactory disorders

- **Anosmia:** complete loss of smell.
- **Hyposmia:** reduced sense of smell.
- **Hyperosmia:** increased sensitivity to smell.
- **Parosmia / dysosmia:** distorted smell perception.
- **Phantosmia:** smelling an odor that is not present (olfactory hallucination).

Common causes include nasal congestion, head trauma (shearing of olfactory fibres), infections, and ageing.

questions.text: List the components of the vestibular apparatus.
questions.keyConcept: Three semicircular canals (cristae) and the otolith organs (utricle and saccule, with maculae), filled with endolymph.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Components of the vestibular apparatus

Part of the membranous labyrinth of the inner ear, filled with endolymph:
- **Three semicircular canals** (lateral, anterior, posterior), each with a dilated **ampulla** containing a **crista ampullaris**.
- **Two otolith organs:** the **utricle** and the **saccule**, each containing a **macula**.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Enumerate the function of each component of the vestibular apparatus.
questions.keyConcept: Semicircular canals: angular acceleration. Utricle: horizontal linear accel/tilt. Saccule: vertical linear acceleration.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Functions of the vestibular components

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| Semicircular canals (cristae) | Detect **angular (rotational) acceleration** in three planes |
| Utricle (macula) | Detects **horizontal linear acceleration** and **static head tilt** |
| Saccule (macula) | Detects **vertical linear acceleration** |

Together they maintain **equilibrium, posture, and gaze stability** (vestibulo-ocular reflex).

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Compare the structure of crista ampullaris with that of otolith organ.
questions.keyConcept: Crista: cupula, no otoliths, detects rotation. Macula: otolithic membrane with calcium otoliths, detects linear
questions.modelAnswer:
### Crista ampullaris versus otolith organ (macula)

| Feature | Crista ampullaris | Macula (otolith organ) |
|---|---|---|
| Location | Ampulla of each semicircular canal | Utricle and saccule |
| Gelatinous cap | **Cupula** | **Otolithic membrane** |
| Otoliths (statoconia) | Absent | Present (calcium carbonate crystals) |
| Adequate stimulus | Angular (rotational) acceleration | Linear acceleration and gravity (tilt) |

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Describe the mechanism of stimulation of crista ampullaris and that of macula.
questions.keyConcept: Crista: endolymph inertia deflects cupula. Macula: heavy otoliths shear hair cells; bending toward kinocilium
questions.modelAnswer:
### Mechanism of stimulation

**Crista ampullaris (angular acceleration):**
- During head rotation the **endolymph lags behind** (inertia) and **deflects the cupula**, **bending the hair-cell stereocilia**.

**Macula (linear acceleration/gravity):**
- The **heavy otoliths** make the otolithic membrane **drag** during linear acceleration or head tilt, **shearing the stereocilia**.

In both, bending **toward the kinocilium depolarizes** the hair cell (increased firing); bending away **hyperpolarizes** it (decreased firing).

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Discuss nervous connections of vestibular apparatus.
questions.keyConcept: Hair cells to vestibular ganglion to vestibular nuclei and cerebellum; project to cord, eyes (MLF), reticular
questions.modelAnswer:
### Nervous connections of the vestibular apparatus

- Hair cells to the **vestibular (Scarpa) ganglion** to the **vestibular nerve** (part of cranial nerve VIII).
- Fibres reach the **vestibular nuclei** (pons and medulla) and pass directly to the **cerebellum** (flocculonodular lobe).
- The vestibular nuclei project to:
  - **Spinal cord** (vestibulospinal tract) for **posture and muscle tone**.
  - **Eye-movement nuclei** via the medial longitudinal fasciculus for the **vestibulo-ocular reflex**.
  - **Cerebellum** for coordination.
  - **Reticular formation / autonomic centres** (nausea, vomiting).
  - **Cerebral cortex** for **conscious awareness** of position and movement.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: List the methods of stimulation of semicircular canals.
questions.keyConcept: Angular acceleration/deceleration (rotation), caloric (warm/cold water) stimulation, and galvanic stimulation.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Methods of stimulating the semicircular canals

- **Angular acceleration or deceleration** (natural rotation of the head).
- **Caloric stimulation:** running warm or cold water into the external ear sets up **convection currents** in the endolymph.
- **Galvanic (electrical) stimulation** of the vestibular nerve.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Outline the mode of actions of semicircular canals.
questions.keyConcept: Detect angular acceleration via endolymph inertia deflecting cupula; respond to change in rotation, not constant
questions.modelAnswer:
### Mode of action of the semicircular canals

- They respond to **angular (rotational) acceleration**, not to constant velocity.
- When rotation starts, the **endolymph lags by inertia** and **deflects the cupula**, bending the hair cells and changing firing.
- They are arranged in **three mutually perpendicular planes**, so any rotation is detected.
- Each canal is **paired with the one in the same plane on the other side**, working in **push-pull**: as one is excited the other is inhibited.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Enumerate the effects of angular acceleration.
questions.keyConcept: Sensation of rotation, nystagmus, past-pointing, falling tendency, vertigo, and autonomic effects (nausea, sweating).
questions.modelAnswer:
### Effects of angular acceleration

- **Sensation of rotation** (and vertigo).
- **Nystagmus** (rhythmic eye movements).
- **Past-pointing** (deviation when pointing).
- A **tendency to fall** toward one side.
- **Autonomic effects:** nausea, vomiting, pallor, and sweating (motion sickness).

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Explain the causes and the sensations of rotation detected at: the start, continuation with constant speed, and at the end of rotation.
questions.keyConcept: Start: cupula deflected, sense rotation. Constant speed: cupula returns, no sensation. Stop: cupula deflects opposite.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Sensations during rotation

- **At the start:** the endolymph lags by inertia and **deflects the cupula**, giving a **sensation of rotation in the direction of the turn**.
- **During constant-speed rotation:** the endolymph **catches up** with the canal, the cupula **returns to rest**, and there is **no sensation of movement** (you feel stationary).
- **At the end (sudden stop):** the moving endolymph **continues by inertia**, deflecting the cupula in the **opposite direction**, giving a **sensation of rotating the other way**, with post-rotatory nystagmus.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Define vertigo. List its physiological mechanisms, and list its other causes.
questions.keyConcept: Vertigo: false sensation of movement; physiological from sensory mismatch; pathological from labyrinth/vestibular
questions.modelAnswer:
### Vertigo

**Definition:** a false sensation of movement (usually spinning) of oneself or the surroundings.

**Physiological mechanisms:** a **mismatch** between vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive inputs, e.g. **motion sickness**, height vertigo, and after **excessive rotation**.

**Other (pathological) causes:** benign positional vertigo, **labyrinthitis**, **Meniere disease**, vestibular neuritis, acoustic neuroma, and central (brainstem or cerebellar) lesions.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Define nystagmus, its components, mechanism and causes.
questions.keyConcept: Nystagmus: rhythmic eye oscillation with slow vestibular phase and fast corrective phase; from rotation or vestibular
questions.modelAnswer:
### Nystagmus

**Definition:** an involuntary, rhythmic to-and-fro oscillation of the eyes.

**Components:**
- A **slow phase**, driven by the vestibular system (eyes drift one way).
- A **fast (corrective) phase** in the opposite direction, generated centrally; it **names the direction** of the nystagmus.

**Mechanism:** an exaggerated **vestibulo-ocular reflex** during or after rotation/caloric stimulation.

**Causes:** physiological (rotation, caloric, optokinetic) and pathological (vestibular, cerebellar, or brainstem lesions, drugs).

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Explain the autonomic and the muscle tone changes that accompany acceleration.
questions.keyConcept: Autonomic: nausea, vomiting, sweating, pallor. Muscle tone: vestibulospinal adjustments altering postural/extensor tone.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Autonomic and muscle-tone changes with acceleration

**Autonomic changes** (via vestibular connections to the reticular formation and autonomic centres):
- Nausea, vomiting, sweating, pallor, salivation, and changes in heart rate and blood pressure (motion sickness).

**Muscle-tone changes** (via the vestibulospinal tract):
- Reflex adjustment of **postural tone** to maintain balance, typically **increased extensor tone** on one side, producing the tendency to **fall or past-point** toward the slow-phase side.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Discuss the functions of utricle.
questions.keyConcept: Utricle: detects horizontal linear acceleration and static head tilt (gravity); aids posture and head-position sense.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Functions of the utricle

- Its macula is oriented **horizontally**.
- Detects **horizontal linear acceleration** (e.g. a car starting forward).
- Detects **static head tilt** relative to gravity, signaling **head position**.
- Contributes to **postural reflexes** and the maintenance of equilibrium.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Discuss the functions of saccule.
questions.keyConcept: Saccule: detects vertical linear acceleration and vertical head tilt; contributes to posture and gravity sensing.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Functions of the saccule

- Its macula is oriented **vertically**.
- Detects **vertical linear acceleration** (e.g. moving up or down in an elevator).
- Detects **head tilt in the vertical plane** relative to gravity.
- Contributes to **posture** and the sense of gravity, complementing the utricle.

questions.text: Explain how you can not detect movement during traveling at 1000 miles / hour in a jet plane, but you can detect the start and the end of movement in a car.
questions.keyConcept: Vestibular receptors detect acceleration, not constant velocity; steady jet speed gives no stimulus, car start/stop
questions.modelAnswer:
### Why constant high speed is not felt, but starting/stopping is

- The vestibular receptors (semicircular canals and otolith organs) respond to **acceleration (a change in velocity)**, **not** to constant velocity.
- In a jet at a **steady 1000 miles/hour**, the velocity is **unchanging**, so the endolymph and otoliths are at rest relative to the head, giving **no stimulus and no sensation** of motion.
- In a car, **starting and stopping** involve **acceleration and deceleration**; the endolymph and otoliths lag behind, stimulating the receptors, so the **start and end of movement are felt**.

*Ai Generated Model Answer*

questions.text: Explain why it is dangerous to swim or dive in water for persons with defective labyrinthine functions.
questions.keyConcept: Without labyrinth and with no visual/gravity cues underwater, the diver cannot tell up from down and may swim downward.
questions.modelAnswer:
### Danger of diving with defective labyrinthine function

- Normally the **labyrinth** signals the direction of gravity and keeps a person oriented.
- **Under water** the usual **visual and pressure/gravity cues are lost or misleading**, so orientation depends heavily on the vestibular apparatus.
- A person with **defective labyrinthine function cannot tell up from down**, may become **disoriented and swim downward** instead of to the surface, and risks **drowning**.

questions.text: Which of the following cortical areas is responsible for the fusion of retinal images?
questions.explanation: Area 17 (primary visual cortex) perceives visual sensations and color vision and fuses the two images formed on both retinae. Area 4 is the primary motor area; area 8 is the frontal eye field; area 18 interprets the meaning of visual sensations; area 6 plans motor movements.
questions.keyConcept: Area 17 (primary visual cortex) fuses the images from both retinae

questions.text: Rods are characterized by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Rods mediate scotopic (dim-light) vision: they are highly sensitive to light, lie in the peripheral retina, and have a high degree of convergence, but cannot detect detail or color. Cones dominate the fovea and mediate photopic and color vision.
questions.keyConcept: Rods are very sensitive to light (scotopic vision)
options: They are responsible for photopic vision
They are the dominant receptors in the fovea
They are responsible for color vision
They are very sensitive to light
They have a low degree of convergence

questions.text: The optic disc is:
questions.explanation: The optic disc is where the optic nerve exits; having no photoreceptors it is the physiological blind spot and is insensitive to light. The central retinal vessels pass through it, and maximum visual acuity is at the fovea.
questions.keyConcept: Optic disc has no photoreceptors, so it is insensitive to light
options: Where condensation of photoreceptors is found
The site of maximum visual acuity

questions.text: A structure not involved in visual accommodation is:
questions.explanation: Accommodation increases the refractive power of the eye for near vision: the ciliary muscle contracts, the zonules slacken, and the lens becomes more convex. The retina is the photoreceptive layer and plays no mechanical role in accommodation.
questions.keyConcept: The retina is not involved in accommodation

questions.text: A 30-year-old man complained of severe headache; his intraocular pressure was 33 mmHg. Which of the following explains this condition?
questions.explanation: Normal intraocular pressure is 12-20 mmHg. Aqueous humor drains at the iridocorneal angle via episcleral (~90%) and uveoscleral (~10%) outflow; narrowing this angle reduces drainage and raises pressure. Increased drainage, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors and parasympathomimetics all lower pressure, and the vitreous is not a determinant of intraocular pressure.
questions.keyConcept: Narrowing the iridocorneal angle reduces aqueous outflow and raises IOP
options: Intake of a drug that inhibits carbonic anhydrase

questions.text: Which of the following is encountered following an oculomotor nerve lesion?
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve drives medial convergence (medial rectus), pupillary constriction (sphincter pupillae) and ciliary muscle contraction, the three components of the near reflex needed to read. After a lesion the pupil is dilated and the eye drifts laterally, while far vision is unaffected.
questions.keyConcept: Oculomotor lesion impairs accommodation, so near reading is blurred
options: Inability to read a book clearly

questions.text: Which of the following conditions causes mydriasis?
questions.explanation: The oculomotor nerve supplies the constrictor pupillae; after a lesion the pupil dilates under the unopposed dilator pupillae. Pontine hemorrhage causes pinpoint pupils, Horner syndrome and muscarinic agonists cause miosis, and alpha-blockers cause miosis.
questions.keyConcept: Oculomotor lesion leaves the dilator unopposed, causing mydriasis

questions.text: Which of the following describes the optic disc?
questions.explanation: The optic disc lies about 3 mm medial to the posterior pole and is the site where the optic nerve exits. Having no photoreceptors, it is the physiological blind spot; the highest visual acuity is at the fovea.
questions.keyConcept: Optic disc is the physiological blind spot (no photoreceptors)
options: It is present in the center of the visual field
It is the site of the highest visual acuity
It is called the physiological blind spot
It contains both rods and cones

questions.text: On fundus examination, the optic disc showed extensive cupping. Which of the following can be the cause?
questions.explanation: The optic cup normally occupies about 0.3-0.4 of the disc. Extensive cupping indicates raised intraocular pressure, as in glaucoma. Raised intracranial pressure (tumor, hemorrhage, CSF defect) instead causes optic disc swelling and papilledema, not cupping.
questions.keyConcept: Disc cupping reflects raised intraocular pressure exceeding intracranial pressure

questions.text: Which of the following is a function of the bony ossicles?
questions.explanation: The auditory ossicles act as a lever system that amplifies (magnifies) sound pressure transmitted from the tympanic membrane to the oval window.
questions.keyConcept: The auditory ossicles amplify (magnify) sound
options: Serve to keep the pressure on the two sides of the tympanic membrane equal

questions.text: Which of the following substances will elicit the sensation of sour taste?
questions.explanation: Sour taste is produced by hydrogen ions (acids). Alkaloids give a bitter taste and amino acids contribute to umami and savory sensations.
questions.keyConcept: Sour taste is elicited by hydrogen ions (acids)

questions.text: Which of the following best describes endolymph?
questions.explanation: Endolymph fills the scala media and is unusual in having a high K+ and low Na+ concentration (intracellular-like). Perilymph (scala tympani and scala vestibuli) resembles extracellular fluid with a high Na+ concentration.
questions.keyConcept: Endolymph has a high K+ concentration

It is present in the scala vestibuli
It is similar in composition to ECF
It has a high K+ concentration

questions.text: A lesion in area 18 leads to which of the following?
questions.explanation: Area 18 (visual association cortex) interprets the meaning of what is seen; its lesion causes visual agnosia, the inability to recognize objects despite intact sight. Complete blindness or hemianopia follow area 17 or visual pathway lesions.
questions.keyConcept: Area 18 lesion causes visual agnosia

questions.text: Which of the following events helps the eye to adapt to night vision?
questions.explanation: Dark adaptation increases retinal sensitivity through regeneration of rhodopsin, mainly in rods. The pupil dilates rather than constricts, bleaching is the opposite of regeneration, and visual acuity decreases as vision becomes rod-dependent.
questions.keyConcept: Night vision depends on increased retinal sensitivity (rhodopsin regeneration)

questions.text: Which of the following characterizes the primary auditory cortex?
questions.explanation: The primary auditory cortex (Brodmann areas 41 and 42 in the temporal lobe) recognizes pitch, loudness and direction of sound. Area 22 is the auditory association cortex, whose lesion causes auditory aphasia and which gives meaning to sound.
questions.keyConcept: Primary auditory cortex recognizes pitch, loudness and direction of sound
options: It is present in Brodmann area 22
It is present in the occipital lobe
It is important for recognition of pitch, loudness & direction of sound
Its lesion leads to auditory aphasia
It is important to understand the meaning of the sound

questions.text: A 15-year-old boy suffers from malnutrition and has vitamin A deficiency. Which of the following is a result of this deficiency?
questions.explanation: Photopigments are formed of retinal (the aldehyde of vitamin A) combined with opsin. Vitamin A deficiency lowers 11-cis-retinal and rhodopsin, raising the visual threshold and reducing retinal sensitivity, so dark adaptation (rod-dependent night vision) is impaired before color vision is affected.
questions.keyConcept: Vitamin A deficiency impairs dark adaptation (night blindness)

questions.text: The equilibrium center is present in the:
questions.explanation: Conscious awareness of equilibrium is represented in the contralateral parietal cortex, where vestibular information is finally projected.
questions.keyConcept: The conscious equilibrium center is the contralateral parietal cortex

questions.text: The fovea contains a high proportion of:
questions.explanation: The fovea centralis is densely packed with cones with minimal convergence, giving the highest visual acuity and color discrimination.
questions.keyConcept: The fovea is densely packed with cones

questions.text: Which of the following is the receptor for color?
questions.explanation: Cones contain the three photopsins responsible for color (photopic) vision; rods mediate only achromatic dim-light vision.
questions.keyConcept: Cones are the photoreceptors for color vision

questions.text: Which structure is responsible for changing the curvature of the lens?
questions.explanation: Contraction of the ciliary muscle slackens the suspensory zonules, allowing the elastic lens to increase its curvature for accommodation.
questions.keyConcept: Ciliary muscle contraction changes the curvature of the lens (accommodation)

questions.text: Which of the following is the visible range of the electromagnetic spectrum for the human eye?
questions.explanation: The human eye perceives wavelengths of roughly 400-700 nm; shorter (ultraviolet) and longer (infrared) wavelengths are not visible.
questions.keyConcept: The human visible spectrum is about 400-700 nm

questions.text: When a rod is stimulated by light:
questions.explanation: Light activates rhodopsin then transducin then phosphodiesterase, lowering cGMP and closing Na+ channels. The reduced Na+ influx hyperpolarizes the rod (a graded potential, not an action potential), decreasing glutamate release.
questions.keyConcept: Light closes cGMP-gated Na+ channels, hyperpolarizing the rod
options: The rod cell generates an action potential
The plasma membrane of the rod cell becomes hyperpolarized

questions.text: A 28-year-old man describes a 6-month history of increasing night blindness. Two of his maternal uncles have the same condition. Visual examination reveals marked constriction of the peripheral visual field. (a) What is your diagnosis? (b) What could be seen on funduscopic examination? (c) What is the inherited pattern of this condition? (d) Justify the clinical findings.
questions.keyConcept: RP: rod degeneration → night blindness + peripheral field loss; bone-spicule pigment; often X-linked.
questions.modelAnswer:
**(a) Diagnosis:** Retinitis pigmentosa (RP).

**(b) Funduscopic findings:** Peripheral *bone-spicule* (perivascular) pigment accumulation, attenuated/narrowed retinal arterioles, and waxy pallor of the optic disc.

**(c) Inherited pattern:** Genetically heterogeneous — may be autosomal recessive, autosomal dominant or X-linked recessive. Affected *maternal uncles* here point to an **X-linked recessive** pattern.

**(d) Justification:** RP is a group of inherited diseases affecting rhodopsin. Rods (concentrated in the peripheral retina) degenerate first → **night blindness** and progressive **peripheral (tunnel) field constriction**; cones are affected later with eventual central vision loss.

questions.text: A boy from Sudan presents with bilateral eye irritation and itching; examination reveals photophobia, conjunctivitis, and fibrovascular opacity in the superior cornea, with cytoplasmic inclusion bodies on Giemsa staining. (a) What term describes the lesion? (b) Justify the presence of inclusion bodies. (c) What are the pathologic features of the disease in its different stages? (d) What is the most serious complication of this disease?
questions.keyConcept: Trachoma stages: follicles → pannus → scarring → trichiasis; complication = corneal blindness.
questions.modelAnswer:
**(a) Lesion:** Trachoma — a chronic keratoconjunctivitis caused by *Chlamydia trachomatis*.

**(b) Inclusion bodies:** *Chlamydia* is an obligate intracellular bacterium that multiplies within conjunctival epithelial cells, forming intracytoplasmic (Halberstaedter–Prowazek) inclusion bodies seen on Giemsa stain.

**(c) Pathologic features by stage:**
- *Stage I:* follicular conjunctivitis with epithelial inclusions.
- *Stage II:* papillary hypertrophy and corneal **pannus** (fibrovascular ingrowth).
- *Stage III:* conjunctival scarring (Arlt line).
- *Stage IV:* diffuse scarring → entropion and trichiasis.

**(d) Most serious complication:** Corneal scarring and opacification leading to **blindness**.

(a) What is the most likely diagnosis? (b) What is the cell of origin? (c) Describe the tumor microscopically. (d) Compare the prognosis of this (uveal) tumor site with the cutaneous origin of the same tumor.
questions.keyConcept: Uveal melanoma: melanocyte origin; spindle + epithelioid cells; hematogenous spread to liver (no uveal lymphatics).
questions.modelAnswer:
**(a) Diagnosis:** Uveal **malignant melanoma** (the most common primary intra-ocular malignancy in adults).

**(b) Cell of origin:** Melanocytes of the uvea (neural-crest derived).

**(c) Microscopic description:** Two cell types — **spindle cells** (spindle A: slender, no nucleoli; spindle B: plumper with small nucleoli) and **epithelioid cells** (large, polygonal, abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with large prominent eosinophilic nucleoli). Variable melanin pigmentation. Epithelioid-cell tumours carry the worst prognosis.

**(d) Prognosis vs cutaneous melanoma:** The uvea lacks lymphatics, so uveal melanoma spreads **hematogenously**, characteristically to the **liver**, often after a long interval. Cutaneous melanoma spreads via both lymphatics and blood and tends to metastasize earlier and more widely.
